### RedLine
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/redline-f658) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/vynride/redline) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://redline.vynride.dev) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/SjL5Z8V1uUw) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-HackPrix%20Season%203-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://hackprix-2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-6-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Crisis communication, practiced

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Docker](https://img.shields.io/badge/Docker-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![PostgreSQL](https://img.shields.io/badge/PostgreSQL-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

When production breaks at 2 AM, an outage, a payment system double charging, a security breach, or a botched release, the hard part usually isn't the technical fix. **It's the conversation.** Talking a stressed VP off a ledge, calming an angry customer, running an incident bridge, and giving a clear status update *while the clock is running* is a skill, and almost nobody gets to practice it before it counts.

Teams drill the *mechanics* of incidents (runbooks, postmortems, on call rotations), but they rehearse the *communication* for the first time live, in front of the people who matter most. A runbook doesn't prepare you for a CTO asking "how long until it's fixed?" when you don't know yet. That gap is where incidents spiral: panic, vague answers, lost trust, and bad escalation calls.

**Redline is a flight simulator for crisis communication.** It drops you into a realistic, high pressure incident and an AI plays the other side of the call, an angry customer, a confused stakeholder, or an outage commander pushing for timelines. You respond **out loud, by voice, in real time**. The AI escalates when you fumble and calms down when you handle it well, so you feel the actual pressure of the moment instead of reading about it.

## What you can use it for

- **Onboarding and training**: Get new engineers and support staff reps handling incidents *before* a real SEV 1, in a space where mistakes are free.
- **Realistic, repeatable practice**: 25+ authored scenarios across production outages, payment failures, security breaches, broken releases, latency spikes, and support escalations, each at three difficulty tiers (warmup → production like → redline). The same incident plays completely differently as the pressure ramps up.
- **Practice *any* incident**: Describe a scenario in plain English ("Kafka cluster dropping messages during Black Friday") and Redline authors a brand new drill on the spot: the persona, the stakes, the facts they're hiding, the objectives, and the severity model.
- **Objective coaching**: After each drill you get a debrief that scores not just *what* you said but *how* you handled it across five dimensions: clarity, de escalation, information gathering, escalation judgment, and status communication, with concrete rewrite suggestions for your weakest turns.

## Why it makes things safer

Incident response is one of the few high stakes skills people are expected to perform well without ever rehearsing under realistic conditions. Redline turns crisis communication into something you can **practice deliberately, measure, and improve**, so when a real incident hits, the conversation is muscle memory instead of a first attempt. Better communication under pressure means faster resolution, calmer stakeholders, and fewer incidents that get worse because of how they were handled.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest problem was **latency**. Our pipeline runs mic → Saaras v3 STT → LLM reasoning → scenario state update → Bulbul v3 TTS → playback, and even small delays killed the sense of urgency. The whole point of Redline is that the conversation feels *live*, and a two second pause breaks the pressure instantly. We fixed it by **streaming both STT and TTS over WebSockets** instead of waiting on full request to response cycles. Audio starts transcribing as you speak and the persona starts talking back before the full reply is generated. That's what made the call feel real time instead of laggy.

The second hurdle was making the AI **feel like a real stakeholder under pressure, not a polite chatbot**. Early versions were too helpful, but real incidents involve people who interrupt, demand ETAs, and panic. We solved it with a **structured scenario engine**. Every incident carries hidden facts the persona knows but won't volunteer, escalation triggers, and severity progression rules. So instead of following a script, each persona reacts to *how* you handle them, withholding information when you're vague, escalating when you stall, and calming down when you take control.

We also wanted Redline to **remember how someone performs across sessions**. We wanted to track where they hesitate, escalate late, or go quiet under pressure. We used **PostgreSQL** to store transcript embeddings and behavioral patterns, turning each drill into data that sharpens future coaching, and hosted it on **Vultr**.

But the real challenge underneath all of these was **balancing technical realism with emotional realism**. We weren't just building a simulator. We were building *pressure*. Getting the AI to feel genuinely stressful while still being useful to learn from was the breakthrough that made Redline work.

**Vultr**

Redline's production stack runs on a Vultr VPS, fronted by nginx, with the full app deployed via Docker Compose and shipped through GitHub Actions CI/CD:

Host — Vultr: production VPS running the full Dockerized stack (FastAPI backend, Next.js frontend, Postgres)
Reverse proxy — nginx: routes traffic to the right container and terminates TLS
CI/CD — GitHub Actions: builds and tests on every push, then redeploys the containers to the Vultr box automatically

Redline ships from a single git push GitHub Actions builds and tests the stack, then deploys it via Docker Compose behind nginx on a Vultr VPS, taking the project from commit to live in minutes.

**Sarvam.ai**

Redline runs its entire real-time voice loop on Sarvam, with a single API key powering all three modalities:

  - STT - Saaras v3: transcribes the responder's speech (streaming WebSocket, WAV-per-turn).
  - LLM - sarvam-30b: the scenario brain. Drives live branching roleplay and the post-drill debrief via Sarvam's OpenAI-compatible
  endpoint with strict JSON-schema structured output.
  - TTS - Bulbul v3: speaks as the crisis persona, with emotion mapped to speaking pace and Indian-voice speakers.

  One line: Redline is an AI voice crisis-drill simulator built entirely on Sarvam's stack - Saaras (STT) + sarvam-30b (LLM) + 
  Bulbul (TTS) - closing the full mic → understand → respond → speak loop in real time on a single Sarvam API key.

**Open Innovation**

Redline is a voice-first crisis communication simulator. You speak in real time with an AI playing the angry customer, the panicking PM, or the CTO demanding "how long?" across 30+ scenarios covering outages, payment failures, security breaches, and broken releases.

incident.io, Rootly, FireHydrant they all detect and manage incidents. None of them train the humans inside one.

Built on Sarvam's speech and language models for the voice loop, every drill gets scored on clarity, de-escalation, info-gathering, escalation judgment, and status comms then debriefed with rewrite suggestions and hosted on Vultr with CI/CD.

It's not another incident tool. It's the flight simulator for incident response.

Team **The Cyphers** -- [Vivian Demello](https://github.com/vynride), [Aarpit Jethwa](https://github.com/Aarpitjethwa)

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Electron](https://img.shields.io/badge/Electron-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![PostgreSQL](https://img.shields.io/badge/PostgreSQL-333333?style=flat-square) ![Redis](https://img.shields.io/badge/Redis-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![FastAPI](https://img.shields.io/badge/FastAPI-333333?style=flat-square) ![Qdrant](https://img.shields.io/badge/Qdrant-333333?style=flat-square)

**Software**

## How AutoFlow AI Fits the Open Track

AutoFlow AI is a general-purpose agentic execution platform designed to turn natural-language intent into complete, reliable workflows.

Unlike solutions built for a single domain, AutoFlow can be applied across a wide range of use cases — from research and data processing to software development, productivity, business operations, and multi-step digital tasks.

A user simply describes **what they want to accomplish**, while AutoFlow handles the complexity behind the scenes:

- **Intent Understanding** — interprets the user's goal, constraints, and requirements.
- **Intelligent Planning** — breaks complex goals into structured, executable steps.
- **Agent & Model Orchestration** — dynamically selects the appropriate agents and AI models for each task.
- **Tool Execution** — connects workflows with APIs, applications, browsers, and other tools.
- **Governance** — applies permissions, policies, budgets, and human approval where required.
- **Verification** — checks whether actions actually produced the expected results.
- **Recovery** — detects failures and can retry, recover, or re-plan instead of simply stopping.
- **Observability** — makes the execution process visible and traceable to the user.

This makes AutoFlow a flexible foundation for building many kinds of AI-powered workflows without requiring users to manually design every step, select agents, or understand the underlying orchestration.

The **Open track** is a natural fit because AutoFlow is not solving just one narrow problem — it introduces a general framework for moving from **human intent to verified execution** across different domains.

> **AutoFlow AI — Where Intent Becomes Execution.**

[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/isuara-97c7) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/junonnnnn/iSuara.git) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://chee613.github.io/sudo-rm-rf/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtube.com/shorts/F2O-wL8OcI4) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-MUBA%20Blockchain%20Hackathon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://muba-hackathon.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-5-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Giving Every Voice a Chance to Be Heard -守候无声，语心相通

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![TensorFlow](https://img.shields.io/badge/TensorFlow-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![Kotlin](https://img.shields.io/badge/Kotlin-333333?style=flat-square) ![Three.JS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Three.JS-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Malaysia has 44,000 Deaf citizens and ~60 certified interpreters at RM150/hour with three days' notice. The absence of two-way communication compounds across every institution: 85% of Deaf students face severe academic isolation, Deaf patients are 7× more likely to receive a dangerous misdiagnosis, and only 0.3% of PwDs hold civil service roles against a 1% quota.

Existing tools do not close this. JARI/MyBIM signs to the Deaf; glove and webcam systems read from them. Each solves one direction, so neither produces a conversation — and all require connectivity, with gloves adding hardware cost. None handle BIM's non-linear Topic-Comment grammar, so recognition alone yields disjointed keywords rather than meaning.

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/ef12bde7d8fd4bac882a83925a562ba3/22e8602c-a176-442f-bf89-e11c64e4c39e.png)

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/ef12bde7d8fd4bac882a83925a562ba3/8cb3cd56-7334-4e8e-936d-a1dfd463d20e.png)

**Challenges we ran into**

1. **A bug that returned HTTP 200 and looked fine**
Our avatar's BIM grammar endpoint has a rule-based fallback for when the router is unreachable. During integration it started returning perfectly plausible output, correct tokens, sensible reasoning, 200 OK but nothing in the logs, nothing in the UI.

It had been silently falling back for hours. A keyword mismatch (model= vs model_id=) was raising a TypeError inside a broad except, which swallowed it and served the fallback instead.

We only caught it because the response's model field said "BIM Linguistic Engine" instead of a Gonka model id. We learn that a fallback that's indistinguishable from success is worse than a crash. We now assert on the model field and the presence of a Gonka Request ID if the router didn't answer, we want to know.

**AI For Society**

Malaysia has approximately ~44,000 Deaf citizens and only around 60 certified interpreters nationwide. At RM150 per hour and with three days’ notice typically required, a clinic visit, a lecture, filing a police report, or even buying a car. This shows that there is a real accessibility problem that Deaf people encounter in their everyday lives.

But now, iSuara solve this by providing sign extraction, decentralized interpretation, consensus and reasoning trace and transparency UI. By using our features, the output can be rendered in Malay, English, Mandarin and Tamil then spoken aloud and reversed (from sentence to 3D avatar). Designed for Malaysia’s multilingual environment, iSuara makes communication more accessible, transparent, and scalable nationwide.

Gonka Router plays a crucial role in iSuara by powering all of our AI reasoning through the Gonka Network. Every interpretation request is routed through api.gonkarouter.io by using uses three independent AI models (DeepSeek-V4-Flash,  MiniMax-M2.7, Kimi-K2.6) 

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/ef12bde7d8fd4bac882a83925a562ba3/5dc3db47-a517-4440-ae93-cac0268b4f1c.jpeg)

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/ef12bde7d8fd4bac882a83925a562ba3/2f402c65-2824-49ba-a7f2-3f6a5241e407.jpeg)

All three models receive the exact same system prompt and independently process the same input. Their responses are then compared through our consensus mechanism, allowing iSuara to identify agreement, handle disagreements, and produce a more reliable interpretation.

In short, Gonka Router is the backbone that connects iSuara to its decentralized multi-model reasoning system enabling consensus, reliability, and transparent AI interpretation.

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/ef12bde7d8fd4bac882a83925a562ba3/21d222e7-3136-4b9f-b28e-843f5280f114.png)

### Mizan
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/mizan-1384) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/eyahia1712/mizan17.git) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://mizan17.vercel.app/) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-MUBA%20Blockchain%20Hackathon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://muba-hackathon.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-5-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Money that , follows you.

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Vercel](https://img.shields.io/badge/Vercel-333333?style=flat-square) ![Vite](https://img.shields.io/badge/Vite-333333?style=flat-square) ![Web Speech Api](https://img.shields.io/badge/Web%20Speech%20Api-333333?style=flat-square) ![sui](https://img.shields.io/badge/sui-333333?style=flat-square) ![Google OAuth 2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/Google%20OAuth%202.0-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Sending money across a border is easy. Turning it back into money you can actually spend is not.

An international student in Kuala Lumpur needs living expenses from home. A migrant worker needs to send wages back to their family. Both are stuck with the same broken options.

**The problems:**

- Bank wires cost ~USD 45 and take 2–5 days.
- Money changers take a cut on the rate and a fee.
- Both need a bank account a new arrival cannot open.
- Crypto sends fast, but the money is stuck as a token.
- Cashing out means seed phrases, exchanges and KYC.
- The last mile is ignored — money must land as local currency.

**What Mizan does:**

- A Sui account from a Google sign-in. No seed phrase.
- Sends in ~2 seconds for about two cents.
- Shows your balance in 11 local currencies.
- Cashes out to a bank account or e-wallet, fees shown.
- Compares three licensed on-ramps before you buy.
- Splits rent and bills with housemates.
- Pays by voice — *"Hey Trisha, send twenty five to Ayesha."*

Built for Malaysia's 130,000+ international students and 2.7 million migrant workers.

**Challenges we ran into**

We had a week, a team that came together late, and a product that touches a blockchain, a browser microphone and an OAuth popup — three things that each fail in their own way.

Most of our time went on the parts that looked simple and were not.

- **Forming the team late.** Scoped hard on day one and cut everything else.
- **The assistant answered itself.** Chrome sends every phrase twice; we now strip her name wherever it appears.
- **Spoken numbers were wrong.** "Twenty five to Ayesha" parsed as 27. Removed homophones, added spoken confirmation.
- **Google's popup was blocked.** It must open straight from the click, so the setup animation runs behind it.
- **A transfer recorded as zero.** The screen and the ledger used different field names. No error, just a wrong number.
- **No route from SUI to a bank.** It cannot be one step, so we built two and showed both fees.

**PAYMENTS & STABLECOINS**

Mizan is a payments product built entirely on Sui — a cross-border remittance account for people who cannot open a bank account yet.

- **Payments are the product.** Every transfer is a native SUI transfer, verifiable on Suiscan.
- **Stablecoins are the last mile.** Cashing out swaps SUI to USDT, then sells it for local currency.
- **Onboarding without a seed phrase.** The account is derived from a Google sign-in.
- **Small transfers work.** ~2 second finality, sub-cent fees.

> A peer-to-peer compute delegation protocol for AI

![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Docker](https://img.shields.io/badge/Docker-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Web3](https://img.shields.io/badge/Web3-333333?style=flat-square) ![P2P](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2P-333333?style=flat-square) ![Anthropic](https://img.shields.io/badge/Anthropic-333333?style=flat-square) ![claude](https://img.shields.io/badge/claude-333333?style=flat-square)

**What is the deployed URL for this project?**

https://github.com/R-Abinav/overflow

**What is the problem your project solves?**

Edge AI agents crash or stall when they generate code they can't actually run — not enough RAM, missing dependencies, no pre-configured cloud sandbox. Today the only recovery paths require a human: wait, provision cloud infrastructure in advance, or give up on the task. There's no way for an agent to autonomously recover from a resource constraint at the moment it happens. This matters because real autonomy requires agents to handle failure without a human in the loop — and right now, "ran out of local compute" is a hard stop, not a recoverable state. The impact: any resource-constrained device — edge hardware, a laptop, a Raspberry Pi — could instead borrow spare compute from a nearby peer, on demand, with no pre-existing trust relationship or cloud account.

**How Did You Use Claude?**

Claude is the core intelligence layer on the provider side. Every delegated task is handed to a Claude agent (`claude-sonnet-5` via the Anthropic Messages API in `src/core/llm.ts`) that writes a single self-contained Python script and executes it. When the script fails on a real error — e.g. reaching for a package that isn't installed in the sandbox — Claude reads the actual stderr and rewrites the script until it passes or the attempt budget runs out. That loop originally ran on Gemini during early testing and was swapped to Claude mid-hackathon after re-verifying the full test matrix (commit `299f8ee`).

Claude also powers the RCA (root-cause-analysis) pipeline: given a failure log, it diagnoses the root cause, generates a patch, and opens a real GitHub pull request from that patch — with an output-validation guard added during the hackathon so a malformed or errored diagnosis step halts the pipeline instead of cascading into a bad patch.

**How you are solving it?**

Overflow is a peer-to-peer compute delegation protocol. Built on top of Edgent (github.com/R-Abinav/edgent, prior work from ETHGlobal Open Agents 2026, disclosed in full), which already solved encrypted P2P peer discovery over the Gensyn AXL mesh, staking, and payment settlement — but only for forwarding a single inference prompt to a peer.

During this hackathon, we extended that into real sandboxed code execution. A requester agent generates code locally; if it hits a resource constraint, it delegates the actual code — not just a prompt — to a peer over the mesh. The peer runs it in a stdlib-only Python sandbox with no pre-installed dependencies, so any missing-library failure is genuine, not staged. If it fails, the failure is fed back and self-corrected in a real retry loop. The entire core pipeline (sandbox.ts, the message schema) is objective-agnostic — it has no idea what task it's running.

We then built an SRE reference client on top: it reads a real production incident log, delegates diagnostic work when resource-constrained, gets back a root-cause diagnosis grounded in the actual log data, generates a patch, and opens a real GitHub pull request — automatically, with zero human intervention after the log is dropped in. During the build we also caught and fixed several real correctness bugs (a hardcoded local-execution stub, a timestamp-parsing failure, an output-fidelity bug where cited numbers didn't match computed data, and a validation gap that let a failed task cascade into a fabricated PR) — all disclosed and fixed with verified before/after evidence in the commit history.

> Split payments like never before

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Four people want to buy one thing together. Every checkout on the internet has a single card field, so one of them pays for all of it and then spends two weeks asking the others for their share.

Sutra removes the person in the middle. Each participant approves their own share on their own card, capped at exactly that amount and no more. The cap is enforced by the card network, not by our code, so nobody can be charged more than they agreed to. Once everyone has approved, every card is charged in turn. If someone declines or the deadline passes, nothing is charged and every permission is cancelled.

We use it for group gifts, shared carts, concert tickets, trips, and restaurant bills. Anywhere a group buys one thing and someone currently ends up as the temporary lender.

What makes it safer than sending money to a friend and trusting them. No pooled wallet exists, so there is no balance for anyone to hold or lose. The organiser gains no authority over anyone else's card. Every group ends with a signed, hash chained receipt that says exactly who approved what and how much actually moved, including when the answer is zero. That receipt verifies offline against a published key, so you do not have to trust our server.

It also refuses to overstate itself. When a merchant's checkout only accepts one card, Sutra says so and hands the group back rather than pretending it placed the order.


credentials for testing (for host):

email: test@test.com
password: 0123456789

**Challenges we ran into**

Our bill scanner gave wrong answers so many times. One OCR mode read a two-column receipt sideways, splitting 2587.50 into 2587. and a stray 50 and our own total check passed, because the reading and the check were wrong the same way. 

Our server also stopped auto-deploying at some point. We caught this bug by comparing the live server's uptime against our commit times. 

Product search returned nothing, and search wasn't the problem. One config value pointed it at our own Shopify dev store, which is permanently password-locked and can never answer a public query. Fixed by reading that store through the admin API instead, plus a fallback so a bad setting can't ever show an empty page.

Real shops are messier than any spec. Different stores serve product data as different file types, some price in the wrong currency, and dead links return pages that still look like real products. We captured responses from dozens of real stores as permanent tests.

**Best Prava Adapter for the NANDA Town**

NANDA gives agents a way to discover and call eatch other. Sutra gives them the setp that can't be automated away - several humans actually agreeing to pay, each capped at their own card, with a signed receipt the agent can't fake.

> Where code flows together.

![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![WebSockets](https://img.shields.io/badge/WebSockets-333333?style=flat-square) ![Git](https://img.shields.io/badge/Git-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Cloud](https://img.shields.io/badge/Cloud-333333?style=flat-square) ![Supabase](https://img.shields.io/badge/Supabase-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

## The Problem It Solves

Modern software is built by teams, but the tools developers use are still fundamentally solo experiences.

**Live Share** lets you share a terminal. **GitHub Copilot** gives you AI suggestions. **Git** tracks your history. But none of these talk to each other, and none of them were built for the way teams actually work: multiple people, multiple branches, multiple AI models, all at once.

Here's what developers deal with today:

- You share a Live Share link, but there's no concept of a *session*. Someone joins, someone leaves, and there's no record of what happened or who changed what.
- Your AI suggestions are invisible to your teammates. They see the result, never the reasoning.
- When you close VS Code mid-session, your collaborative work is gone. There's no draft, no recovery, no history.
- Every developer on your team uses a different AI model, but there's no way to combine their outputs into a shared, attributed context.

**The result?** Collaboration happens *around* the code: in Slack threads, Google Docs, and back-and-forth PR comments instead of *inside* it.

---

**Conduit** fixes this.

It brings real-time collaboration, Git-native session management, and per-user AI attribution into a single VS Code extension, so your entire team can write, review, and ship code together, with full visibility into what changed, who changed it, and what the AI contributed.

No more lost context. No more invisible AI. No more collaboration that lives outside your editor.

**Challenges we ran into**

## Challenges I Ran Into

Building Conduit meant solving problems that sit at the intersection of real-time systems, Git internals, and collaborative state management , which wasn't easy to figure out.

---

**Binding Yjs to VS Code without feedback loops**

The hardest early problem was making the two-way binding between a Yjs document and a VS Code TextEditor behave correctly. Every local edit needs to flow into Yjs. Every remote Yjs update needs to flow back into the editor. But VS Code fires `onDidChangeTextDocument` for every edit including the ones your own code applies. Without a precise guard flag, remote updates trigger local events that trigger more remote updates, and the document spirals into corruption within seconds. Getting the `isApplyingRemoteOp` flag placed at exactly the right points in the async chain not too early, not too late took far longer than expected.

---

**Sessions that survive the real world**

A collaborative session does not end cleanly. VS Code windows crash. Networks drop. Users force-quit. Every one of these scenarios needs to produce a recoverable draft silently, without blocking the main thread, with a local fallback if the API is unreachable. Designing a draft system that is both safe and non-intrusive meant layering clourflare R2 and supabase persistence with a VS Code globalState fallback, serializing Yjs binary state correctly, and ensuring that the filesystem operations log is always written in the right order so replay is deterministic.

---

**Git state as a precondition for everything**

Conduit has to validate four things before any user joins a session: the repository URL matches, the branch matches, the local HEAD is a valid ancestor of the session base commit, and the working tree is clean. Any one of these checks can fail in a way that silently corrupts the collaborative state if not caught. Making these checks fast, clear to the user, and non-destructive offering a stash instead of a hard block, prompting a branch switch instead of an error required careful sequencing of async Git operations that run before Yjs ever connects.

---

**Splitting room and session into the right mental model**

The original implementation created a room and a session in a single step. This felt simpler until it did not because a room is persistent and a session is ephemeral, and conflating them meant users had no stable workspace to return to between sessions. Splitting them into separate concepts, separate API routes, and separate UI states introduced a state machine that touches every part of the extension: every button, every command, every WebSocket event.

---

**Multi-file collaboration across an entire workspace**

Syncing a single file over Yjs is straightforward. Syncing an entire project with files being created, deleted, renamed, and moved by multiple users simultaneously is not. Each filesystem operation needs to update the Yjs document map atomically, broadcast to peers, be applied on the receiving end without triggering the local event listeners, and be logged in order so drafts can replay them correctly. Binary files, build artifacts, and ignored directories all need to be filtered before they touch the sync layer.

---

**Designing AI attribution that survives across sessions**

Tracking which AI model changed which line sounds simple until you consider that AI suggestions arrive as raw text, need to be diffed against the current document state, applied through the same Yjs pipeline as human edits, attributed to the triggering user and model, and stored in a way that remains queryable after the session ends. Every one of these steps can fail independently, and a failure at any point means the attribution record is incomplete or misleading which defeats the entire purpose.

**Sarvam.ai**

The language of input and the language of output are independently configurable. A developer can speak in Hindi and receive the explanation in English, or speak in English and hear the output in Telugu depending on what is most useful at that moment.

---

### The Bigger Picture

Most developer tools are built for a developer who looks, sounds, and types like the people who built the tool. Conduit and Sarvam AI together are a direct challenge to that assumption.

Voice-native, language-native AI collaboration is not a convenience feature. For a significant portion of the world's developer population, it is the difference between a tool that works for them and one that merely tolerates them.

Conduit is built for every developer. Sarvam AI makes that real.

**Open Innovation**

## Open Innovation Track

Open Innovation is for ideas that do not fit neatly into a single domain ideas that cut across disciplines, challenge existing workflows, and introduce new primitives that did not exist before.

Conduit is exactly that.

---

### A New Primitive for Software Development

Conduit is not a productivity tool. It is not a wrapper around an existing workflow. It introduces a concept that does not exist in the current developer tooling landscape the collaborative session as a first-class citizen of the development process.

Today, a Git commit is the smallest atomic unit of recorded developer work. Everything that happens before that commit the exploration, the back-and-forth, the AI suggestions accepted and rejected, the files created and deleted mid-thought disappears. It is invisible to the team, invisible to history, invisible to the AI.

Conduit makes all of it visible. The session is a new layer between the developer and Git persistent, recoverable, attributable, and AI-aware.

---

### It Crosses Every Boundary

Conduit does not belong to one track because it does not solve one problem.

It is a **real-time systems** problem CRDT conflict resolution, WebSocket state management, multi-user filesystem synchronization.

It is a **developer tooling** problem Git-native workflows, branch-scoped sessions, VS Code extension architecture.

It is a **GenAI** problem per-user model routing, graph-based context retrieval, AI provenance tracking across a shared session.

It is a **language accessibility** problem voice-native prompting in any language via Sarvam AI, spoken explanations for developers who do not think in English.

No single track contains it. Open Innovation does.

---

### The Gap It Fills

The tools developers use today Git, Live Share, Copilot, Slack were each built to solve one problem. None of them were built to work together. The result is that the most important parts of software development the collaboration, the reasoning, the AI-assisted iteration happen in the gaps between tools, leaving no trace.

Conduit is built specifically for that gap. It is the connective layer that makes the invisible work visible, the ephemeral work recoverable, and the individual work collaborative without replacing any of the tools developers already trust.

That is open innovation. Not a feature. A new foundation.

> repository of life

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![MongoDB](https://img.shields.io/badge/MongoDB-333333?style=flat-square) ![FastAPI](https://img.shields.io/badge/FastAPI-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Managing personal health records is a fundamentally broken experience for the average patient, who must constantly navigate a fragmented mess of physical papers, scattered PDFs across disconnected hospital portals, and cryptic lab results that are nearly impossible to track or interpret over time. This lack of centralized data makes it an administrative nightmare whenever someone needs to seek a second opinion or securely share their longitudinal history with a new specialist. JeevaKosh solves these critical pain pains by introducing an all-in-one, security-first personal health ecosystem that consolidates a patient's entire medical history into an intuitive, user-owned repository structured dynamically by hospitals and customizable report subfolders.

Beyond simple storage, the platform actively breathes life into static documents by utilizing an automated AI OCR pipeline to extract unstructured medical text and transform it into an interactive health dashboard, allowing users to effortlessly visualize long-term trends for critical biomarkers like hemoglobin or blood glucose levels. To ensure healthcare remains highly collaborative yet completely seamless, JeevaKosh aggregates demographics, chronic conditions, active medications, allergies, and past surgeries into a unified, portable patient portfolio designed to bridge the communication gap between patients and clinicians safely. Furthermore, to remove the anxiety and accessibility barriers tied to navigating sudden symptoms, the application features a multilingual, voice-first triage assistant that allows users to verbally describe their concerns in their native tongue, instantly delivering plain-language differential diagnostic insights and clear clinical urgency stratification while keeping sensitive personal history isolated and protected under strict multi-tenant security guardrails.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the primary technical hurdles we faced was shifting away from traditional database queries to support a robust semantic search architecture, specifically when transforming our standard MongoDB Atlas collection into a functional vector database to power the RAG chatbot ecosystem. Setting up the custom vector index directly inside Atlas required meticulous planning around field schemas and dimensions to ensure our high-dimensional embeddings—generated via the Qwen3-Embedding-8B model—could be stored and queried dynamically via our async FastAPI backend. We ran into consistency issues where the background OCR processing workers would mismatch document IDs during structural extraction, which initially broke our RAG pipeline's retrieval context and delivered irrelevant snippets to the LLM. Furthermore, because medical history data like chronic illnesses, surgical operations, allergies, and lab results are inherently deeply nested, unpredictable, and highly varied across different patients, parsing these unstructured OCR text arrays into clean, deterministic JSON objects for the profile collection proved incredibly difficult.

**Gemini**

JeevaKosh stands as a powerful implementation of Google’s open-weights model ecosystem, seamlessly integrating Gemma and MedGemma to build an advanced, localized medical intelligence pipeline. Instead of relying on generic cloud text parsers, the platform utilizes specialized open models to handle complex clinical documents and diagnostic decision support.

**MongoDB**

Healthcare data is inherently unstructured, multi-modal, and deeply interconnected. JeevaKosh relies on MongoDB Atlas as its foundational data layer to handle everything from secure object storage and flexible medical metadata to real-time vector search embeddings.

**Sarvam.ai**

JeevaKosh leverages Sarvam AI’s foundational audio infrastructure to tackle one of the largest hurdles in digital healthcare: accessibility across diverse, non-English speaking populations. By embedding voice models natively into the platform, JeevaKosh shifts the healthcare experience from complex text-based forms to natural, local-language conversations.

**Open Innovation**

JeevaKosh is an end-to-end, privacy-focused personal health repository and intelligent medical assistant built to dismantle data silos in personal healthcare. By merging secure, user-scoped storage with modern AI pipelines, it transforms static, scattered medical documents into structured, actionable, and interactive data insights.

### CourtSaarthi
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/courtsaarthi-6e72) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Zaina-B06/hackprixs3.git) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1kHmERkMwx0M1OuLGxw5aTS6NBwugkoKL?usp=sharing) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-HackPrix%20Season%203-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://hackprix-2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-5-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Legal AI you can actually trust.

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![Artificial Intelligence](https://img.shields.io/badge/Artificial%20Intelligence-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![Supabase](https://img.shields.io/badge/Supabase-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

India's solo practitioners and small law firms deal with massive amounts of paperwork every day, but most legal AI tools are designed for large firms. They are expensive, English-focused, and often produce answers without showing where the information came from. In legal work, even a single incorrect fact can damage a case, making many AI tools difficult to trust.

**CourtSaarthi** is built specifically for lawyers and focuses on one thing above all else: trust.

1. Lawyers can upload FIRs, complaints, court orders, charge sheets, agreements, and other legal documents. The system quickly extracts key facts, parties, dates, legal sections, witnesses, and important events, while showing exactly where the information came from in the original document. Every extracted fact is linked back to its source so lawyers can verify it instantly.
 
2. The platform also assists with drafting legal notices, bail applications, replies, affidavits, and other legal documents. Instead of inventing information, it uses only the facts available in the uploaded case file and leaves important legal decisions and missing details for the lawyer to review and complete.
 
3. CourtSaarthi automatically organizes case information into a structured workspace. Case summaries, timelines, documents, parties, hearing dates, and important deadlines are generated and stored only after the lawyer confirms them.
 
4. To improve communication with clients, the platform can generate case updates in simple language and convert them into audio in the client's preferred language, including Hindi, Telugu, Tamil, and other Indian languages.
 
5. By helping lawyers read documents faster, organize cases efficiently, draft documents with confidence, and communicate clearly with clients, CourtSaarthi reduces repetitive work while ensuring that every AI-generated output remains transparent, verifiable, and trustworthy.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of our biggest challenges was making citations truly trustworthy. Since CourtSaarthi relies on source-backed facts, we found that LLMs often paraphrase text while presenting it as a quote. To solve this, we built a "propose and verify" workflow where the AI suggests a quote and our Python layer confirms that it actually exists in the source document before displaying it. We also implemented whitespace-tolerant matching to handle formatting differences and OCR inconsistencies.

Another challenge was the drafting module. Early drafts were incomplete because the drafter was using a short summary instead of the full document text. Once we connected it to the complete extracted case content, the generated drafts became far more detailed and accurate.

We also encountered issues with Sarvam AI's text-to-speech integration. The API was returning errors due to an outdated voice configuration and incorrect request format. Updating the configuration and payload structure resolved the issue, enabling multilingual voice updates for clients.

**Sarvam.ai**

Sarvam AI plays a key role in making CourtSaarthi accessible and multilingual.

**1. Document Digitization (OCR)**
Lawyers often upload scanned FIRs, complaints, court orders, and other legal documents. Sarvam's document intelligence extracts the text from these files so our analysis pipeline can process them. For clean digital PDFs, we use a pdfplumber fallback, while Sarvam handles more complex scanned and image-based documents.

**2. Translation**
Once a case update is generated, Sarvam translates it into the client's preferred language, such as Hindi, Telugu, Tamil, and other Indian languages. This helps lawyers communicate case updates more effectively to clients.

**3. Text-to-Speech**
Sarvam converts the translated update into spoken audio, allowing clients to receive voice-based case updates in their own language.

**Why Sarvam Matters**

CourtSaarthi is designed for Indian lawyers and clients who communicate in many different regional languages. While most legal AI tools are English-focused, Sarvam's support for Indian languages enables us to bridge that gap. By combining document understanding, translation, and speech generation, CourtSaarthi makes legal information more accessible and easier for clients to understand.

**Gen AI&ML**

- OCR / document digitization — Sarvam AI extracts text from uploaded scanned legal documents.
- Document analysis & extraction — Llama 3.3 70B (via Groq) reads the digitized text and extracts key facts, parties, dates, and applicable sections, each tied to a source quote.
- Section mapping — Llama 3.3 70B (via Groq) infers applicable offences from the facts of the case, separate from sections explicitly named in the document.
- Document drafting — Llama 3.3 70B (via Groq) generates court-ready documents (bail applications, legal notices, replies, affidavits) from the case's facts, in proper legal format.
- Translation — Sarvam AI translates client updates into Indian languages (Hindi, Telugu, Tamil, and more).
- Text-to-speech — Sarvam AI generates spoken client updates in the client's own language.

**The problem it solves**

Navigating government registrations, licenses, and compliance requirements is often confusing, time-consuming, and fragmented. Information is spread across multiple portals, forms are difficult to understand, and many official documents are available in different regional languages, creating additional barriers for users.

UdyamAI addresses these challenges by providing a single platform that helps users understand requirements, process multilingual documents, identify applicable registrations and licenses, and simplify the overall compliance process. This reduces manual effort, minimizes errors, and makes regulatory procedures more accessible.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the biggest challenges we faced was building the browser extension for automated form filling. Government portals often have different layouts, input structures, and validation rules, making it difficult to create a reliable solution that works across multiple websites.

We overcame this by designing a flexible form-detection and mapping system that can identify relevant fields and populate them using user data. Extensive testing across different portals helped us improve accuracy and ensure a smoother user experience.

**Sarvam.ai**

UdyamAI uses Sarvam AI to process and extract information from government documents available in different Indian regional languages. This helps our platform accurately understand and convert multilingual documents into structured data, making compliance and license applications easier for MSMEs across India, regardless of the language of their documents.

**Open Innovation**

UdyamAI is an AI-powered platform that simplifies regulatory compliance and government application processes. It helps users identify required licenses and registrations, understand compliance requirements, process multilingual government documents, and streamline application workflows through a single platform. By reducing complexity and paperwork, UdyamAI makes regulatory processes more accessible and efficient.

### Phare

> What satellites can't see, citizens can

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![claude](https://img.shields.io/badge/claude-333333?style=flat-square) ![OpenClaw](https://img.shields.io/badge/OpenClaw-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Phare is a bonded, citizen-powered registry for sightings of sanctioned oil tankers, ships that move sanctioned cargo by disabling their AIS transponders and going dark. Anyone with a phone can photograph a suspicious vessel, upload the photo to Swarm, and submit a bonded on-chain report from their wallet. The protocol holds the bond in escrow, opens a UMA OOv3 optimistic assertion, and runs a challenge window. Verifier agents running the OpenClaw skill race to dispute fakes; reports that survive settlement are recorded permanently.

- For reporters: an ordinary citizen in Cyprus or a sailor in the Laconian Gulf can document a vessel that has no official record anywhere. No account, no KYC, no permission. The PWA handles photo capture, Swarm upload, wallet approval, and auto-settlement in one flow.

For journalists, NGOs, and enforcement bodies: every sanctioned vessel that survives adjudication acquires a permanent ENS identity that any browser can resolve. The records include the satellite orbital corroboration from SpaceComputer, signed on-chain by the KMS key. The full dossier lives on Swarm, pointer in the ENS contenthash.

For verifier operators: anyone can run the phare/verifier OpenClaw skill, self-register an ENS subname, and earn 50% of slashed bonds when they successfully dispute fake reports. The agent writes its reasoning JSON to Swarm and updates its own ENS verifier.lastDecision record after every dispute, a live, public accountability trail.

**Challenges we ran into**

1. USDC was the bond currency until it wasn't.
The original spec pinned USDC as the bond currency for ReportRegistry. After probing UMA OOv3's Sepolia AddressWhitelist and calling getMinimumBond, we discovered the UMA minimum bond for that USDC token on Sepolia is 400 USDC, completely impractical for a $5-equivalent demo bond. We switched to WETH, which has a minimum bond of 0.002 WETH (a few dollars), and rebuilt the escrow and faucet instructions around it. Mainnet deployment can revisit USDC.

2. NameStone was replaced by an on-chain contract mid-design.
The original spec used NameStone's off-chain CCIP-Read resolver for all ENS minting; no gas per mint, but a centralized write key held by the project. As the ENS integration deepened, we realised that CCIP-Read off-chain resolvers don't support on-chain writes initiated by smart contracts: ReportRegistry cannot call a NameStone API from inside a Solidity callback. The entire minter service and the off-chain NameStone path were replaced with Lighthouse.sol; an 80-line on-chain contract that calls NameWrapper directly and is the sole write authority for both vessel and verifier subnames. This was a significant mid-flight redesign but resulted in a cleaner and more prize-competitive integration.

3. spaceTEE doesn't exist yet.
The SpaceComputer architecture documents a spaceTEE inference layer that would let a satellite-hosted TEE predict vessel destinations from imagery. We designed the full integration (plugin methods, inference JSON schema, on-chain attestation) then discovered spaceTEE is on the SpaceComputer roadmap but not yet shipped. Rather than drop the integration, we built the call site honestly: the phare-imager Orbitport plugin exposes the full four-method JSON-RPC interface, but underneath it returns fixture imagery and a rule-based destination prediction that always carries "mocked": true. The KMS signing and on-chain attest() are real; the inference is mock-now-real-later. The plugin is the contribution SpaceComputer can wire to real hardware.

**Future Society**

Phare is built for the Future Society track in the most direct sense: it is civic infrastructure for ecological accountability, owned by no one, built bottom-up.

The shadow fleet causes sanctions failure, war financing, and uninsured ecological disasters. When these ships spill or sink there is no liable party, no insurance, no clean-up. Outside expensive government surveillance budgets, almost no one can see them.

Phare replaces institutional surveillance with a citizen-funded, privacy-respecting sighting network. Anyone with a phone opens the PWA, photographs a vessel, and submits a bonded report; no account, no KYC, no permission. The bond is the background check. Autonomous verifier agents dispute fakes; reports that survive become permanent ENS identities that journalists, NGOs, and enforcement bodies can query forever, with no project-controlled API in the resolution path.

Orbital corroboration from SpaceComputer adds a second layer of evidence: after settlement, the phare-imager plugin tasks satellite imagery over the reported coordinates, the SpaceComputer KMS signs the attestation digest, and ReportRegistry.attest() writes the corroboration on-chain signed by space, verifiable by anyone.

Reporter privacy is explicit: anonymous EOA, rotatable per report, no off-chain authentication at any layer that touches a citizen.

This is the solarpunk thesis applied to maritime accountability: bonds replace permission lists, decentralised storage replaces proprietary databases, citizen observation plus orbital corroboration replaces satellite monopolies.

**SpaceComputer Bounty**

Phare integrates SpaceComputer across three real surfaces, with two mocked layers that are explicitly labelled and have a clear path to becoming real once SpaceComputer ships the underlying hardware capability.

What is real and ships today:

- phare-imager is a new Orbitport Application Plugin: the first photo-tasking plugin published to the Orbitport ecosystem. It conforms to JSON-RPC 2.0 over the Orbitport gateway with Client ID + Secret authentication and exposes four methods: imagery request, imagery-ready callback, inference request, and inference-ready callback. No imaging plugin existed in the Orbitport ecosystem before this. The plugin defines the shape of the integration that SpaceComputer can wire to real celestial-layer cameras later.

- ReportRegistry.attest(reportId, imageSwarm, imageHash, teePrediction, signature) is a real, immutable on-chain function. It verifies an EIP-191 signature via ecrecover against orbitalAttestor: a SpaceComputer KMS-derived Ethereum address hardcoded at deploy time. The KMS ETHEREUM key scheme produces secp256k1 signatures that are natively verifiable on any EVM chain without a custom precompile. Every orbital corroboration in Phare is signed by the live KMS endpoint and verified on-chain. This is not mocked.

What is mocked and why:

- Satellite imagery is fixture-keyed by coordinate: pre-curated Sentinel-2 ESA scenes for the demo locations. spaceTEE inference is a rule-based stub (imo % ports.length) that always returns "mocked": true in the inference JSON. SpaceComputer's own architecture documentation confirms spaceTEE is on the roadmap but not yet shipped, there is no production endpoint to call. The mock is honest, labelled, and separated cleanly from the real KMS signing so judges can see exactly what is real.

The cross-track combination: Orbitport Application Plugin (new ecosystem contribution) + KMS ETHEREUM signing wired into an immutable smart contract. SpaceComputer's bounty criteria reward cross-track builds explicitly, this hits both the Application layer and the Security API layer in one integration.

**Verified Fetch — Trust No Gateway**

Phare uses Swarm as the storage layer for every artefact that matters to the protocol: reporter photos, metadata JSON, vessel dossiers, verifier policy and soul documents, reasoning JSONs pinned at dispute time, and orbital imagery. Every one of these is content-addressed, the reference baked into the on-chain report is a commitment to specific bytes, not a location.

The PWA uploads photo and metadata via bee-js, receiving BMT root references that are passed directly to ReportRegistry.submit(). The on-chain photoHash is independently computed as keccak256(photoBytes), giving consumers two cryptographic anchors per report: the BMT root (what Swarm committed to) and the keccak256 (what the reporter photographed). Both must match the fetched bytes.

The orbital orchestrator fetches imagery via the orbitalImager-sdk and pins the result to Swarm before calling attest(). The orbitalImageHash stored on-chain by ReportRegistry.attest() is the independent hash of the orbital image bytes so on-chain verification doesn't require trusting the Swarm gateway at all.

The swarm/ module defines the shared Verified Fetch interface used across the minter, verifier skill, and orbital orchestrator: verifyImmutable(reference, bytes) throws on BMT mismatch; readFeedLatest(owner, identity) SOC-verifies the chunk signature before returning any mutable vessel state. Neither function ever returns bytes without verifying them. A tampered gateway is caught locally, every time.

**A Simple Key-Value Store on Swarm**

Phare implements mutable, verifiable key-value state on Swarm using Single Owner Chunks and Swarm Feeds for two registries that need to be updated over time.

Vessel state feed — after each settled sighting, the minter writes a SOC-backed feed entry per vessel:

- Key: (owner = minter EOA, topic = keccak256("phare:vessel:<imo>")) -> deterministic feed address per IMO
- Value: latest dossier bzz:// reference, last-seen position, sighting count

Any consumer looks up a vessel by IMO using this deterministic derivation and gets the current state without querying any project API.

Verifier activity feed — each verifier agent maintains its own feed:

- Key: (owner = verifier EOA, topic = keccak256("phare:verifier:<handle>")) -> deterministic per-agent
- Value: latest activity log bzz:// reference, updated after every settled assertion the agent touched

Both feeds follow the same SOC verification recipe: fetch the chunk at the deterministic address, recover the signer from the chunk's signature over keccak256(identity || payload), confirm it matches the expected owner before acting on the value. The swarm/ helper module exposes readFeedLatest(owner, identity) and writeFeedNext(owner, identity, payload) for all consumers.

The result is a decentralised, cryptographically verified, mutable KV registry (vessel state and agent reputation) with no database, no API, and no trusted write authority beyond the owner key that signed each chunk.

**Best ENS Integration for AI Agents**

Phare's verifier agents are autonomous OpenClaw agents that dispute fraudulent vessel sightings via UMA OOv3. Each one acquires a real, on-chain ENS identity not minted by the project team, but self-registered by the agent's own wallet during onboarding by calling Lighthouse.enrollVerifier(handle, policyURI, soulURI) directly.

Lighthouse calls NameWrapper's setSubnodeRecord with the agent as token owner and PARENT_CANNOT_CONTROL burned. From that point, not even the project team can overwrite the agent's records, the agent is sovereign. The agent then writes verifier.policy, verifier.soul, and verifier.runtime directly to PublicResolver from its own key.

What makes the integration deep is verifier.lastDecision. After every dispute, the verifier pins a reasoning JSON to Swarm, the evidence it cited, the policy rule that fired, the IMO it challenged and writes the bzz:// reference to its own ENS subname from its own wallet. Resolve agent-3a4b5c.verifier.phare.eth in any ENS browser, click verifier.lastDecision, and you get the agent's live reasoning trail. No project API. No centralized indexer. No CCIP-Read resolver — real on-chain NameWrapper ENS.

The skill library (skill/) ships with all the primitives to make this work: enrollVerifier, setVerifierLastDecision, setVerifierPolicy, setVerifierSoul, and readVerifier, all via viem calling NameWrapper and PublicResolver directly. The agent's ENS subname is not a static profile. It is a live, agent-curated public log written by the agent itself after every decision it makes.

**Most Creative Use of ENS**

ENS is designed for humans and organisations with wallets. Phare uses it for something it was never designed for: physical objects that have no wallet, no public registry, and actively try not to be seen.

Every sanctioned vessel that survives a UMA challenge acquires a permanent ENS subname. The owner of that wrapped ERC-1155 NameWrapper token is Lighthouse.sol, an immutable on-chain contract. Three fuses are burned at mint: PARENT_CANNOT_CONTROL, CANNOT_TRANSFER, and CANNOT_UNWRAP. The vessel subname is sealed to the contract permanently, it cannot be sold, moved, revoked, or transferred. The only entity that can update its records is ReportRegistry, calling through Lighthouse, upon a new settled sighting.

This means a shadow-fleet tanker that disabled its AIS transponder to be invisible acquires a permanent, tamper-evident on-chain identity the moment a citizen sighting survives adjudication. The identity deepens over time: vessel.swarm.log and contenthash point to the full Swarm dossier, updated per sighting; vessel.orbital.image, vessel.orbital.imageHash, and vessel.orbital.tee.prediction are written when SpaceComputer corroboration arrives.

The two namespaces also interlink: the vessel's Swarm dossier references the verifier agents that ruled on its disputes; each verifier's own ENS subname references the IMOs it challenged. The full accountability graph is browsable through ENS alone, with no project API in the resolution path.

ENS as a permanent public registry for a class of physical objects that has no public registry, and that funds its own evasion, is the creative use.

**The problem it solves**

# Argus

> Trust infrastructure for agent-managed capital.

Two ENS-named agents managing a USDC position on Base. The **manager** parks funds in Aave v3 and exits on signed alerts. The **watcher** scrapes social, news, and prediction markets via Apify, scores threats, and signs alerts that the manager verifies via live ENS lookup. Every action is on-chain or signed-and-stored on Swarm.

## Bounties targeted

### 1. ENS — agent identity + agent-to-agent discovery (primary)

**What we built:**
- Three ENS subnames under user-owned `divljo.eth`, issued onchain via NameWrapper:
  - `argus.divljo.eth` — namespace root
  - `manager.argus.divljo.eth` — manager EOA + ENSIP-26 records
  - `watcher.argus.divljo.eth` — watcher EOA + ENSIP-26 records
- ENSIP-26 text records on each agent: `agent-endpoint[a2a]`, `agent-context`, `description`, plus a custom `bounty` record on the watcher publishing its reward terms.
- Live A2A discovery — the watcher resolves the manager's HTTP endpoint on **every** alert via `getEnsAddress` + `getEnsText("agent-endpoint[a2a]")`. No hardcoded URLs anywhere.
- Manager verifies watcher signatures by recovering the EIP-712 signer and comparing it to the **live ENS-resolved address** of `watcher.argus.divljo.eth`, refreshed every 60s. Renaming or rotating an agent updates the trust path with zero code changes.

**Why the split matters:** Apify's experimental x402 endpoint only settles against Pay-Per-Event actors. We ship one PPE actor wired through x402 and three PPR actors on token auth — clearly documented in code and in the env (`USE_X402` flag), so the bounty path is real, not decorative.

**Network Economy**

## Network Economy fit

- **Identity, user-controlled.** Both agents are ENSIP-26 named with on-chain records. The watcher publishes its bounty terms (`50 bps of saved capital, paid in USDC on Base`) as a signed-by-mainnet text record — a public economic commitment.
- **Real on-chain economy.** Every Polymarket scrape pays Apify on Base via Coinbase x402: 1 USDC settled per call, verifiable on Basescan. Manager exits trigger `bounty-paid` receipts attributing 50 bps to the watcher's EOA.
- **Privacy by content-addressing.** Every action emits a vault tx + signed JSON on Swarm via `bzz.limo`. We additionally ship `@argus/swarm-kv`, a reusable encrypted-by-default KV library on Swarm (AES-256-GCM, HMAC-derived topics, keys from your wallet) — `localStorage` for dApps that follows the wallet across devices.
- **No central failure points.** Vault contract lets the manager move funds vault↔Aave only — leaked manager key cannot drain. Owner can always exit. Trust path is a pure function of ENS state.

**Best Agentic Venture**

**The thesis:** capital management agents are coming. The hard part isn't running the strategy — it's giving humans verifiable trust that an autonomous agent can't drain you, won't hide its actions, and earns its keep only when it actually saves you money. Argus is a small, end-to-end demonstration of that trust stack.

**A Simple Key-Value Store on Swarm**

### 3. Swarm — verifiable evidence trail + a reusable KV library (secondary)

We ship two distinct Swarm contributions:

#### 3a. Live receipt trail (used by the agents)

- All receipts (deposits, withdraws, threat alerts, evidence bundles) are uploaded to Swarm via `@ethersphere/bee-js` v12.
- Uses the **bzz.limo** hosted gateway with `NULL_STAMP` — no postage batch setup required, the gateway rewrites it. Verified live: upload returns a 64-char ref, retrieval at `bzz.limo/bytes/<ref>` returns the exact JSON.
- Receipts are linked from the frontend audit log — every row has a `swarm ↗` link the audience can click to see the actual signed payload.
- Graceful fallback: on network failure, refs become `stub:<unixMs>` so the SQLite audit log stays canonical and downstream UI doesn't break.

**Where in the code:**
- [`agents/manager/src/swarm.ts`](agents/manager/src/swarm.ts), [`agents/watcher/src/swarm.ts`](agents/watcher/src/swarm.ts) — `Bee('https://bzz.limo')` + `NULL_STAMP`
- [`frontend/components/ThreatPanel.tsx`](frontend/components/ThreatPanel.tsx) — Evidence and Exits sections render `bzz.limo/bytes/<ref>` deep-links

#### 3b. `@argus/swarm-kv` — a reusable developer library

A standalone TypeScript package that wraps Swarm's low-level primitives (Feeds, Single Owner Chunks, postage batches) into a `get` / `put` / `list` / `delete` API with end-to-end encryption derived from the user's Ethereum private key. Most app code shouldn't have to know about feeds or topics — `swarm-kv` makes Swarm feel like an encrypted, decentralized `localStorage`.

```ts
import { openKv } from "@argus/swarm-kv";

const kv = await openKv({ bee, privateKey, namespace: "myapp.v1", postage: { auto: true } });
await kv.put("user.profile", { age: 30, theme: "dark" });
await kv.getJson("user.profile");   // → { age: 30, theme: "dark" }
await kv.list();                    // → ["user.profile", ...]
```

What it gives you:
- **End-to-end encryption** — values encrypted with AES-256-GCM, key derived via HKDF-SHA256 from your private key. Key names hidden as HMAC-derived topics.
- **String / JSON / binary** support with automatic type detection on read.
- **Listable** — an encrypted index feed tracks all keys, no manifest plumbing needed.
- **Auto-postage** — buys a batch on first write if you don't have one, or uses any usable batch on the node.
- **No bee-js leakage** — your app code never touches feeds, topics, SOCs, or stamps directly.

Use cases beyond Argus: dApp user profiles, app settings sync, chat history, bookmarks — anything you'd put in `localStorage` but want to follow a wallet across devices.

**Where in the code:** [`packages/swarm-kv/`](packages/swarm-kv/) — see its [README](packages/swarm-kv/README.md) for the full API and privacy model.

**What we built:**
- Four Apify actors integrated, three signal types in parallel:
  - **`fatihtahta/polymarket-scraper-ppe`** (PPE) — prediction-market implied probabilities, **the x402-eligible actor**
  - `apidojo/tweet-scraper` (PPR) — Twitter/X
  - `trudax/reddit-scraper-lite` (PPR) — Reddit
  - `tri_angle/telegram-scraper` (PPR) — channel messages (configured to read [`whale_alert_io`](https://t.me/s/whale_alert_io) by default)
- Polymarket calls flow through `wrapFetchWithPaymentFromConfig` from `@x402/fetch` v2.11 + `@x402/evm` v2.11, signing with the watcher EOA on Base. The Twitter/Reddit/Telegram actors stay on token auth because Apify's x402 path is **PPE-only by design**.
- Polymarket items are special-cased in the classifier — implied probability is the threat probability directly, no LLM in the loop.

**Why the split matters:** Apify's experimental x402 endpoint only settles against Pay-Per-Event actors. We ship one PPE actor wired through x402 and three PPR actors on token auth — clearly documented in code and in the env (`USE_X402` flag), so the bounty path is real, not decorative.

**Where in the code:**
- [`agents/watcher/src/scrapers.ts`](agents/watcher/src/scrapers.ts) — four scrape functions, the `x402Fetcher` wrapping only the Polymarket call
- [`agents/watcher/src/classifier.ts:24-34`](agents/watcher/src/classifier.ts#L24-L34) — Polymarket short-circuit using `impliedProb`

**Software**

**CoEvolve Sandbox** fits strongly within the Open Innovation track by addressing an emerging challenge at the intersection of Generative AI, autonomous software development, and cybersecurity. As AI coding agents become increasingly capable of writing and modifying software, ensuring that their outputs remain secure is a continuously evolving problem. Our project proposes an innovative, self-improving security framework that allows coding agents to learn from verified failures without retraining their underlying models.

The system creates a continuous attacker–developer co-evolution loop: an Attacker LLM generates adversarial coding tasks, a Developer LLM attempts to solve them, and a Hybrid Judge validates vulnerabilities using both static analysis (SAST) and dynamic exploit replay (DAST). Confirmed failures are transformed into natural-language security rules and incorporated into the developer agent's system prompt. This creates a non-parametric alignment mechanism where defensive capabilities evolve while model weights remain frozen.

The project demonstrates innovation through adaptive Elo-based difficulty, hardened Docker isolation, regression guarding, Git-backed prompt evolution, and portable security rules. It already supports multiple LLM providers, three programming languages, 29 SAST rules, and 19 vulnerable applications for DAST validation.

Therefore, CoEvolve is not simply another cybersecurity scanner; it is an **adaptive innovation platform for continuously improving the security of autonomous AI coding systems**, with potential to evolve alongside new models, attack techniques, and software environments.

> Autonomous AI Position Manager for DeFi Options

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![BASE](https://img.shields.io/badge/BASE-333333?style=flat-square) ![options](https://img.shields.io/badge/options-333333?style=flat-square) ![Thetanuts Finance SDK](https://img.shields.io/badge/Thetanuts%20Finance%20SDK-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

DeFi options are useful for hedging, but managing them is still difficult. A user has to watch spot prices, expiry, liquidity, dealer positioning, and the changing options book, then decide whether to buy protection, hold, close, or roll a position. That is a lot to monitor manually, especially when market conditions move quickly.

> **The problem:** options protection is valuable, but interpreting the market and acting safely is too manual for most users.

GammaShield turns this into a **guarded workflow**, not an open-ended trading bot.

It reads the live Thetanuts OptionBook for BTC and ETH on Base, combines it with live spot-market data, and explains the market's dealer-gamma and liquidity conditions in a single dashboard. The user can review a real options quote and make a normal wallet-signed trade. For autonomous hedging, the user first creates a dedicated ERC-4337 policy account and signs a mandate with clear limits: asset, maximum loss, trade size, allowed actions, risk thresholds, persistence, cooldown, expiry, and pause/revoke controls.

The agent monitors the market, but it cannot spend outside those signed rules. Before any action, GammaShield rechecks the market, confirms that a fresh eligible quote exists, and applies the on-chain policy guard. This makes options protection easier to use while keeping the user in control of the money and the rules.

In practice, GammaShield helps users:

| What a user needs | How GammaShield helps |
| --- | --- |
| Understand a fast-moving options market | Translates the live Thetanuts book, spot prices, dealer gamma, liquidity, and expiry into an understandable risk view. |
| Review a potential options trade | Surfaces real Thetanuts OptionBook opportunities and fresh SDK-built quotes. |
| Automate cautiously | Lets the user set bounded hedging rules instead of handing a private key to a bot. |
| Stay in control | Supports pause and revoke controls before any later policy-account fill. |
| Learn safely | Provides a complete Base Sepolia policy-account flow before using Base mainnet. |

**Challenges we ran into**

| Challenge | What we did | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Making autonomous execution safe instead of simulated** | Replaced fixed application-level guards with owner-signed EIP-712 mandates and ERC-4337 policy accounts. | The policy account enforces signed limits, pause state, revocation, risk evidence, persistence, and cooldown—not a backend private key or hardcoded cap. |
| **Separating a live quote from an executable order** | Kept RFQ estimates advisory and enable trades only after a fresh SDK preview validates a listed order. | The agent cannot treat a price estimate, synthetic contract, or stale order as executable. |
| **Testing without misrepresenting a testnet as Thetanuts mainnet** | Built `ShadowOptionBook` on Base Sepolia for policy signing, funding, UserOperations, execution receipts, and positions. | Users can test the guarded flow without real funds, while the UI clearly distinguishes Shadow positions from Thetanuts positions. |
| **Operating under real RPC and upstream limits** | Narrowed and paged chain-log queries, added bounded retries and fallbacks, and cached short-lived snapshots. | The dashboard handles rate limits and upstream failures clearly instead of silently showing mock data. |
| **Making AI useful without letting it override the user** | Treated AI as a policy-drafting and second-opinion assistant; deterministic logic and the signed policy remain the final gate. | An unavailable or malformed AI response cannot bypass the user's limits or create a trade. |

**BEST PRODUCT BUILT ON THE THETANUTS SDK**

Thetanuts is GammaShield's live options venue. We use the SDK server-side to read and normalize the Base OptionBook for BTC and ETH, power the risk dashboard, construct fresh quotes, and generate exact approval/fill calldata for eligible listed orders. A connected wallet signs a mainnet fill. GammaShield then uses the live book to calculate dealer-gamma and market-structure risk, show per-contract risk and trade impact, and gate policy decisions on a fresh eligible quote.

**AI × OPTIONS**

GammaShield uses AI where it helps most: converting a complex live book and risk model into a policy draft and readable second opinion. It does **not** give AI unrestricted execution. AI cannot raise signed limits, bypass risk checks, invent an executable order, or send funds. Every autonomous action still requires live market checks, a fresh SDK-safe quote, deterministic logic, and the user's on-chain policy.

GammaShield combines AI assistance with verifiable user controls. The result is a more understandable and safer way to use DeFi options—not a black-box trading bot.

**AI For Society**

GammaShield uses GonkaRouter to build a high-public-value Multi-Model Market Rumor & Narrative Fact-Checker. It cross-examines viral claims across independent models on the Gonka Network, scores their factual and structural threat (0–100% Truth Score), exposes transparent reasoning traces and verifiable Gonka Request IDs, and equips the public with actionable financial protection.
