### Oronyx
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/oronyx-8ece) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/tsujisalju/oronyx) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FEgplSa2d0w) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/FEgplSa2d0w) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-MUBA%20Blockchain%20Hackathon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://muba-hackathon.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Policy-enforced AI agent wallets on Sui Blockchain

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![FastAPI](https://img.shields.io/badge/FastAPI-333333?style=flat-square) ![move](https://img.shields.io/badge/move-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

AI agents are increasingly being trusted to act autonomously with real money — trading, rebalancing, staking — but almost every "agentic finance" demo today relies on the same weak guarantee: a system prompt or app-level setting telling the agent what it's "supposed" to do. If the agent misbehaves, is prompt-injected, or the backend is compromised, there is nothing structurally stopping it from moving funds outside the user's intent.

Oronyx solves this by moving policy enforcement on-chain. When a user sets up an agent, they describe their rules in plain language — spending limits, which actions are allowed, which targets are whitelisted, how risk-averse the agent should be. This gets compiled into a Move capability object on Sui that structurally gates every action the agent can take. The agent's backend never holds a blank check — it holds a scoped, revocable, on-chain-enforced permission slip.

Concretely, this means:

- An agent literally *cannot* exceed a spending limit, act on a non-whitelisted address, or act past its expiry — not because it was told not to, but because the smart contract will abort the transaction.
- Anything above the user's risk threshold isn't silently auto-executed — it's parked on-chain for the user to explicitly approve or reject.
- The user can edit policy live (tighten a limit, revoke a target, deactivate the agent entirely) at any time, independent of whether the backend is online, trustworthy, or even compromised.

This is useful for anyone who wants the convenience of an autonomous financial agent — a rebalancer, a DCA bot, a staking optimizer — without having to fully trust the software running it.

**Challenges we ran into**

**Cetus testnet had no usable liquidity.** We built a full Programmable Transaction Block integration against Cetus's SDK, expecting to demo a real swap. Systematic testing — discovering real pools, correcting swap direction to match which side of the pool SUI actually sat on, verifying coin decimals — eventually surfaced Cetus's own zero-output abort (code 18) across every SUI-paired testnet pool we could find: the price ratios were too skewed to produce a meaningful output at reasonable test amounts. Rather than keep chasing a moving target, we built our own fixed-rate mock DEX as the demo's primary swap path, and kept the real Cetus integration fully implemented and reachable — a deliberate reliability decision, not an abandoned feature.

**Getting the trust model right took real iteration.** Our first design had the agent's capability object owned by the user's wallet address — which turned out to be a fundamental blocker: an address-owned object can only be used by a transaction that address itself signs, which would mean the user co-signing every single agent action, defeating the point of automation. We restructured to shared objects with explicit owner/operator fields checked in the contract logic instead, which is what actually enables autonomous execution while keeping the user as the sole authority over policy changes and approvals.

**Cetus's SDK doesn't compose the way we assumed.** We initially planned to chain our policy-check function's released funds directly into a Cetus swap call within one atomic transaction. Checking the SDK's actual installed type definitions (rather than trusting the docs) revealed it always builds its own transaction internally and selects its own input coins — there's no way to hand it an existing transaction or a specific coin. We resolved this by scoping the two-step, non-atomic pattern specifically to Cetus, while keeping every other action type (transfer, stake, mock swap) atomic and funds-never-leave-custody by default — this also became one of our core architectural principles going forward.

**Noodles.fi temporarily suspended on-chain API access for retail** We planned to use Noodles.fi API to poll market data in Sui Network, but in unfortunate turn of events, Noodles announced that they are temporarily suspending access to their API dashboard within the time frame of this hackathon. We instead opted to use market data from DeepBook.

**Reliably fine-tuning the agent decision-making to get desired action outcomes** The agent decision-making takes in real market trends data, agent cap, current vault balance and recent activity. Each variable input has to be carefully filtered to ensure predictable outcome for live demo simulation. For example, a long history of failed actions reinforces the agent's decision to withhold from making further actions, requiring clean up of activity logs or filtering redundant activities.

**AI × SUI**

Oronyx is built directly for this track's premise — Sui isn't an add-on storage layer here, it *is* the trust mechanism. The agent's authority is a Move capability object, not a database row; every policy check (spending limit, allowed target, risk threshold) is a contract-level assert, not application logic the agent could be tricked or misconfigured around.

We use several of the track's highlighted Sui features directly:
- **Programmable Transaction Blocks** are central to execution, not incidental — every atomic action type (transfer, stake, mock swap) completes policy-check-and-execute in a single PTB, so funds never leave the vault's custody boundary until they land at their real destination.
- **Sponsored transactions** using Enoki as sponsor remove gas as an onboarding barrier — a first-time user can create an agent and start using it without ever holding SUI themselves.
- **zkLogin** using Enoki service replaces wallet setup with a standard OAuth flow, so "connect" doesn't require the user to already be crypto-native.

The track asks for AI solving a real problem where Sui is integral, with thoughtful UX and a working live demo. Our real problem is trust: letting an AI agent act autonomously with money is currently a leap of faith. Oronyx turns that leap into a structural guarantee, backed by a live demo of an agent executing real policy-gated actions on testnet.

[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/hackmate-ai-aipowered-hackathon-team-builder-8256) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Shubham-Banerjee-2006/ai-hackathon-team-maker) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-MUBA%20Blockchain%20Hackathon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://muba-hackathon.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Smarter Matches. Stronger Teams. Better Hacks.

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![scikit-learn](https://img.shields.io/badge/scikit--learn-333333?style=flat-square) ![Docker](https://img.shields.io/badge/Docker-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![FastAPI](https://img.shields.io/badge/FastAPI-333333?style=flat-square) ![NLP](https://img.shields.io/badge/NLP-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

Turning "skills on paper" into a fair team split was harder than expected. Two 
people can list the same skill tag but mean very different levels of depth, so 
naive keyword matching gave misleading compatibility scores. We had to move 
toward embedding-based similarity and tune the balance between skill coverage 
and shared interest so the optimizer didn't just cluster people with identical 
skills together. Getting the explanation text to stay accurate to the actual 
scores — rather than generic filler — took a few iterations too.

**The problem it solves**

Hackathon teams are usually formed by chance — whoever you happen to sit next to. 
That leads to overlapping skills, missing roles (no one covering design, or no one 
covering ML), and hours lost negotiating groups instead of building.

HackMate AI fixes this. Participants register their skills, interests, role, 
experience, availability, working style, and a short bio. The system uses NLP 
embeddings and skill-complementarity scoring to evaluate how well people's skills 
fit together, then an optimizer generates balanced teams — each with a skill 
coverage score, a compatibility score, and a plain-language explanation of why 
that group works. Participants can also use "Find My Teammates" to get ranked, 
individually-explained matches instead of a full team.

**The problem it solves**

## The Problem TrustMesh Solves

Digitalization is no longer optional for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), yet many are trapped in a standoff that prevents them from taking the necessary risks. On the other side of this gap are Malaysian university students—a massive pool of emerging digital talent. This talent goes unused in the real economy because students must take non-relevant part-time work, like retail or barista jobs, just to survive their studies.

Both sides are paralyzed by a mutual lack of trust.

**The SMEs' problem is risk.** They know they need to digitize to scale, but they cannot afford the high costs of agency development. They want to hire students, but they will not send money up front. They have no cheap way to judge quality before paying, and they fear receiving incomplete work from a student they have never met.

**The students' problem is opportunity.** They need relevant professional experience to launch their careers, but they are terrified of being exploited. A student who builds a website for an SME and gets ghosted has no realistic recourse. Chasing a few hundred ringgit through formal channels costs more than the job is worth. Furthermore, they have no credible way to prove their skills—screenshots and promises don't win the next client.

So the SME remains stagnant, and the student's potential is wasted.

TrustMesh removes the standoff by removing the need for trust. We bridge the opportunity gap by replacing blind faith with a decentralized, automated protocol.

---

## How TrustMesh Unlocks the Standoff

1. **Fund and Prove.** TrustMesh connects to the SME’s existing project management tools to automate job creation. The budget is locked into an escrow vault on the Sui blockchain in the same action. This funds the contract and proves to the student that the money is genuinely secured before they write a single line of code[cite: 1].
2. **Submit and Audit.** The student submits their completed work (links, summaries). TrustMesh leverages Gonka Router, a decentralized AI inference protocol, to act as an independent, impartial auditor[cite: 1]. Gonka compares the delivery against the original brief and scores it[cite: 1].
3. **Automatic Payout.** TrustMesh removes human bias and delays. If the AI review scores the work at 80/100 or higher, the escrow contract triggers an automatic payout in a single transaction: 90% to the student and 10% to the platform.
4. **Verifiable Portfolios.** The part students lack today is evidence. Every completed job on TrustMesh emits a `MilestoneAuditedEvent` on-chain. This permanent, public, and independent blockchain record carries the AI review ID, the score, and the amounts paid. It is the undeniable portfolio proof students need to show they have delivered in real-world scenarios.

---

## Invisible Web3: Built for Everyday Businesses

Small business owners do not want to manage crypto wallets, memorize 12-word seed phrases, or buy volatile tokens. TrustMesh delivers the security of blockchain without the friction:

* **1-Click Google Sign-In:** Both SMEs and students onboard in seconds using their standard Google accounts via Sui zkLogin[cite: 1]. No wallet extensions or private key management required[cite: 1].
* **Zero Gas Fees:** A backend relayer covers all network transactions through sponsored executions[cite: 1]. Users only see their digital dollar balance[cite: 1].
* **Familiar Business Workflow:** The interface functions like a standard project management and milestone portal. The blockchain operates entirely behind the scenes as a secure settlement layer and an immutable audit trail

---

**What this changes for each side**

- **The company cannot quietly walk away.** The money is already committed before the student starts.
- **The student cannot hand in placeholder work.** The review checks the submission against what was actually asked for, not against a promise.
- **Neither side pays a network fee.** A relayer covers gas, so a student never has to acquire SUI to get paid in stablecoins.
- **The rule is not enforced by our interface.** The 80-point gate is an `assert!` inside the Move contract, so it holds even if someone bypasses the app and calls the contract directly.

---

**The part students don't have today**

Every completed job emits a `MilestoneAuditedEvent` on chain carrying the AI review ID, the score and the amounts paid. That record is permanent, public, and independent of us. It is the portfolio evidence students currently have no way to produce, and it survives even if TrustMesh disappears.

---

**Live on Sui Testnet**

- Package: [`0x65220b62...1775ff8`](https://suiscan.xyz/testnet/object/0x65220b620646127a170967e69ebedf0358e328f0c744833f9dde7d00f1775ff8)
- End-to-end run, live AI review scored 81 and the escrow released: [`HKajqi4PVB7...mr83Qej`](https://suiscan.xyz/testnet/tx/HKajqi4PVB7DvUF53vvpocwV3wkauew2Ui3Kwmr83Qej)
- Code: [github.com/jijo-jiji/muba-hack](https://github.com/jijo-jiji/muba-hack)

**Challenges we ran into**

**1. Sui switched off the transport our app was built on, two days before the deadline.**

Our entire frontend stopped talking to the chain at once. Every call came back with:

`Method not found. JSON-RPC on public fullnodes has been deprecated.`

Sui has been retiring JSON-RPC through 2026, and `@mysten/sui`'s `SuiClient` speaks exactly that from the browser. So `getCoins`, `executeTransactionBlock` and `tx.build({ client })` all died together. No environment variable could fix it.

**How we got past it.** Migrating properly to gRPC or GraphQL was a multi-day job we did not have. What saved us was noticing that the Sui CLI still works, because it does not use JSON-RPC. We moved every chain-touching operation behind our own server and had that server drive the CLI:

- on-chain USDC balance reads
- the Mock USDC faucet
- the milestone release itself

It is not the architecture we would ship, and we say so plainly in the README. But it meant a real transaction landed instead of us demoing a mock.

---

**2. We caught our own app inventing proof.**

Our first working build was largely AI-generated. When we sat down and actually read it, we found that whenever a transaction failed, it would:

- generate a random 64-character hex string
- call it a transaction digest
- set the status to `"success"`
- render a SuiScan link that went nowhere

In the same file, execution time was clamped with `Math.min(480, Math.max(160, ...))`, so any slow call displayed as under 500ms while our README advertised sub-500ms settlement as a headline feature.

**How we got past it.** None of it was deliberate. It was demo-safety scaffolding that had quietly turned into a lie. We tore it out and replaced it with an explicit `not_executed` status carrying a plain-language reason, then made one rule non-negotiable:

> No digest and no explorer link ever appears unless a transaction was genuinely confirmed on chain.

That rule then caught two more instances we had missed: hardcoded per-model latencies sitting inside a panel we had named "Transparency Dashboard", and canned AI results that now carry a visible **"Demo data, not a live Gonka call"** badge. The README has a "what is real and what is simulated" table for the same reason.

---

**3. Our demo could not tell its own story.**

We built the product as a single dashboard with a persona dropdown. We only spotted the problem while rehearsing the pitch: our whole argument is a three-party trust story, but the demo was one person clicking every button in one window. The first question any judge would ask is *"wait, who is clicking that?"*

**How we got past it.** We split it into real `/company` and `/student` routes with permissions enforced server-side, including ownership checks so a student cannot reach another student's job by editing the URL. It improved the architecture, but the reason we did it was the pitch.

---

**4. A vault pays out exactly once, which we learned the hard way.**

`release_audited_milestone` sets `is_active = false`, so our second rehearsal aborted with Move error code `103`. That is correct behaviour, since a company should never be charged twice for the same job, but it means every full run consumes a vault.

**How we got past it.** We wrote `scripts/new-escrow-vault.sh` to mint funds and create a fresh vault in one command, and added it to the reset instructions in the README.

---

**5. One hour lost to a signing bug that was not a signing bug.**

The Sui TypeScript SDK wants the raw 32-byte secret key base64-encoded. The Sui CLI exports bech32, starting `suiprivkey1...`. Pasting the CLI output straight into the env file fails in a way that looks like a cryptography problem and is actually a formatting one.

**How we got past it.** Decode first, then re-encode:

`decodeSuiPrivateKey(kp.getSecretKey())` → `toBase64(secretKey)`

**PAYMENTS & STABLECOINS**

TrustMesh moves stablecoin payments between two parties who do not trust each other, without either side needing to hold SUI.

A company funds a job by locking Mock USDC (a 6-decimal test stablecoin, trustmesh::mock_usdc) into a shared EscrowVault object on Sui. There is no such thing as an unfunded job on the platform. When the work passes review, release_audited_milestone pays both parties out of that one vault inside a single transaction: 90% to the student, 10% to the platform treasury. Because it is one transaction, it cannot half-succeed and leave the student paid but the fee lost, or the reverse.

Neither user ever touches gas. A relayer wallet attaches and signs for the network fee, and the user's signature and the relayer's are submitted together. Accounts are addressed by derived Sui addresses rather than a browser wallet extension, so a student signs in without managing a seed phrase.

Deployed and running on testnet. Package 0x65220b620646127a170967e69ebedf0358e328f0c744833f9dde7d00f1775ff8. Example 90/10 payout: 74myhZT5X9mTaD47o8CpuCfBPiYPX9Gy6XvxgCTK3j3Z.

**AI × SUI**

The AI is not a feature bolted onto a Sui app. Its output is what authorises the on-chain call, and Sui is what makes the AI's verdict binding.

When a student submits work, Gonka Router reviews it against the original brief and returns a score out of 100 plus a request ID. Both of those are passed into release_audited_milestone as Move arguments, and the contract itself runs assert!(truth_score >= 80). The gate lives on chain, not in the interface, so it holds even if someone bypasses the app and calls the contract directly. An AI verdict below 80 cannot release money, no matter who is asking.

The contract then emits MilestoneAuditedEvent carrying the Gonka request ID, the score and the amounts alongside the payout. That means every payment on the platform traces back to the specific AI review that justified it, permanently and publicly.

Full end-to-end run where a live review scored 81 and the payout executed: HKajqi4PVB7DvUF53vvpocwV3wkauew2Ui3Kwmr83Qej.

**AI For Society**

Every inference in TrustMesh runs through Gonka Router at https://api.gonkarouter.io/v1. There is no OpenAI fallback and no other provider anywhere in the codebase.

Each submission is checked by two independent models dispatched in parallel: moonshotai/Kimi-K2.6 checks whether everything in the brief is actually present, and deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash checks whether the work is genuinely finished rather than placeholders, TODOs or dummy files. Their scores are combined into a single Truth Score out of 100, shown alongside an itemised reasoning trace and the individual Gonka request IDs for each inference, so a user can see exactly which calls produced their verdict.

The social purpose is specific. Malaysian student freelancers get ghosted after delivering work and have no affordable recourse, while small companies have no cheap way to judge quality before paying. An impartial machine reviewer that neither party controls breaks that standoff. Only the assigned student can trigger a review, so a company cannot quietly re-run it until it gets an answer it prefers.

We also ship /verify, a standalone tool that runs the same multi-model consensus check against any URL or text claim.

**Challenges we ran into**

**Dual-Wallet Architecture & Context Mismatch:**
To deliver a seedless Web2 onboarding experience, we integrated Google zkLogin via Mysten Labs' Enoki SDK. Early implementations ran into state desynchronization issues where browser redirects after Google authentication failed to cleanly restore the user's active session within React context, occasionally triggering null address errors during transaction execution. We resolved this by auditing the @mysten/dapp-kit-react provider hierarchy, standardizing our OAuth callback routes, and building an automated session-recovery hook that deterministically derives the ephemeral keypair and Sui address before enabling transaction actions.

**The problem it solves**

Traditional subscription billing gives merchants unlimited, open-ended authority over your cards or wallets, leading to hidden cancellation mazes, forgotten free-trial charges, and silent price hikes.

Today, **ShieldPass** replaces open-ended billing with programmable, escrow-backed payment passes on Sui. Users set strict boundaries: an authorized merchant, an exact per-charge price ceiling, and an automated expiry date, before funds are locked.

It makes recurring payments safer and effortless by:
- **Eliminating the "Free-Trial" Trap:** Passes self-expire automatically when a trial ends, making surprise renewal charges impossible without having to navigate cancellation mazes.
- **Enforcing Hard Spend Caps:** Any unauthorized price hike exceeding the user's per-charge limit is instantly rejected on-chain by Move smart contract logic.

- **Removing Web3 Friction:** Powered by Enoki Google zkLogin, users get trustless smart-contract protection using standard Google sign-in—with zero seed phrases or complex wallet onboarding.

**PAYMENTS & STABLECOINS**

**ShieldPass** brings programmable consumer protection to recurring digital payments on Sui.

While conventional subscription billing relies on open-ended payment mandates and off-chain trust, ShieldPass leverages Sui’s object-centric architecture to turn subscriptions into self-enforcing, escrow-backed permissions. Users lock deposits directly into a Move smart contract with strict on-chain boundaries: an authorized merchant address, an immutable per-charge price ceiling, and deterministic time expiration powered by the Sui Clock (0x6).

> Market move but We don't

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

Here's the challenges field, same treatment — table for the parallel structure (each is a bug → cause → fix), so it's scannable at a glance:

---

## Challenges we ran into

| Challenge | What happened | How we fixed it |
|---|---|---|
| **The order book that looked ideal was the one we couldn't fill** | Our quote engine returned deep floors (20%+ below spot) at 27- and 62-day expiries for over a week of development — until we tried to actually fill one and got `Panic(0x11)`, an arithmetic overflow that said nothing about *why*. We chased the wrong lead (a missing token approval) before finding the real cause: our order filter was inverted, and those "ideal" floors were orders where *we'd* be the seller, not the buyer. | We started simulating every order against the chain instead of trusting the raw book. The real, fillable market turned out to be ~2–3 day floors around 6% below spot, not 30-day floors at 20% — so we reframed the product around *event protection* instead of quietly shipping a demo that would fail the moment anyone tried to buy from it. |
| **A loan that was under-collateralised the moment it was written** | Our lending product's whole claim is that the credit limit comes straight from the option's strike, no haircut. Our first real loan — 4.5977 USDC lent against a 4.5977 floor — came due owing **4.599410**, more than its own floor. We were lending 100% of the guarantee and *then* charging interest on top of it. | We stopped subtracting interest from the floor and instead solved backwards for the principal that, plus its own interest over the loan's term, lands exactly on the floor (`principal × (1 + rate × days/365) = floor`) — the same technique we already used for the vault's principal-protection split. |
| **A payout silently 10¹² too small** | The SDK uses 6 decimals for an order's own contract count, but 18 decimals for the same-named argument to the payout-calculation helper. Passing one straight into the other doesn't throw an error — it just returns a number a trillion times too small. We only caught it by computing a payout by hand and comparing against the code's answer. | We wrote one dedicated conversion helper (`toPayoutContracts()`) so that decimal boundary gets crossed exactly once, in one place, instead of being a trap every future caller could fall into individually. |

Each of these mattered because it changed *what we could honestly claim about the product*, not just what the code did underneath it.

**The problem it solves**

## The problem it solves

If you hold crypto and the price falls, every option available today costs you something permanent:

- **Sell** — the loss stops, but so does any chance of the rebound. You end up right about the asset and out of the position anyway.
- **Hold** — you absorb the entire fall, with no floor and no plan, hoping it recovers before you need the money.
- **Borrow against it** — and risk getting liquidated the moment the market dips, sold at the worst price of the crash, often hours before the price recovers. The bounce lands for someone else.

A financial instrument that solves exactly this — a put option — has existed for decades. It gives the holder the right to sell at a fixed price, so the downside gets a floor while the upside stays fully open, and the maximum possible loss is capped and known in advance. Options are barely used outside professional trading, not because the instrument doesn't work, but because every interface that offers one demands the user understand strike prices, expiries, implied volatility and theta decay before they can even get a quote. **The instrument was never the barrier — the interface was.**

### What Alpha does

Alpha removes that interface barrier. The user describes what they're worried about in plain language — *"protect my ETH from falling more than 20%"* or *"I need at least $2,000 by 1 November"* — and the app buys real downside protection on their behalf on the live Thetanuts order book on Base mainnet. No strike price, no expiry, no options terminology ever appears on screen.

**Three products, one underlying engine:**

| Product | What it does | The mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| **Protection** | A real on-chain floor under crypto you already hold | Cost, floor and max loss stated in USDC before you confirm — the premium paid is the only number that can go wrong |
| **Lending** | Borrow USDC against that same protected holding, with no liquidation risk | Credit limit = strike × contracts, minus the loan's own interest — never a loan-to-value ratio. A conventional lender discounts collateral and reserves the right to liquidate because it has no floor; Alpha has a floor, so the credit limit *is* the floor |
| **Vault** | A principal-protected deposit | The yield a deposit would normally earn buys a call option instead of being paid out — principal back in full at maturity, plus a share of any rise, computed from the real premium paid, never promised in advance |

**Who it's for:**

| Audience | What they need |
|---|---|
| **Holders** who don't want to sell | A known worst case, stated in dollars, before a volatile event |
| **Borrowers** already liquidated once | Cash without selling — and without handing a lender the right to sell them out again |
| **Savers** who can't tolerate losing principal | Little or no upside is acceptable; losing the deposit is not |

### Why it's real, not a mockup

Every purchase is a fully-collateralised position on Base mainnet, verifiable independently on BaseScan — not a database row backed by a promise. As of submission, eight real transactions are on chain, including a protection purchase, a loan disbursement derived from that exact position's strike, a loan repayment, and a call purchase funding a principal-protected deposit. The one part of the product that is *not* real is the user's starting balance — this is a custodial prototype with no deposit flow, so demo balances are seeded rather than funded, and the interface discloses that boundary at the point each number appears rather than in a disclaimer nobody reads.

### The design rule underneath all three products

**The user is always the buyer of the option, never the seller.** Option buyers have losses capped at the premium and open-ended upside; sellers have capped gains and losses that scale with the size of the position. For a decade, retail users have been quietly steered onto the seller side by products advertising "stable yield" that are structurally the same as selling insurance without underwriting it properly. Alpha does not offer that trade, at any price — which is what makes it safer than the products it's replacing, not just simpler to use.

### SmartSplit

> Define the Rules. Let Sui Move the Money.

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Firebase](https://img.shields.io/badge/Firebase-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Firestore](https://img.shields.io/badge/Firestore-333333?style=flat-square) ![Auth0](https://img.shields.io/badge/Auth0-333333?style=flat-square) ![Vercel](https://img.shields.io/badge/Vercel-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

**Designing around Sui's wallet-controlled transaction model.** The frontend needs to calculate each recipient's share, split the payer's coin, construct the multi-transfer transaction, hand it off for wallet approval, and wait for on-chain indexing, all without SmartSplit ever holding custody of user funds at any step.

**Coordinating the real-world layer around the payment.** The on-chain transfer is only part of the problem. We also had to build friend and community management, payment requests, user profiles, SuiNS resolution, and a way to keep off-chain request status in sync with what's actually confirmed on-chain.

**Receipt handling.** We combined browser-based OCR with decentralized Walrus storage for receipt images, while making sure the detected amount is always shown to the user for verification or correction before they ever sign a transaction. Accuracy has to come before convenience here.

**Validation and rounding.** Equal and custom splits both needed clear validation to catch invalid or incomplete distributions before they reach the chain, along with correct rounding and dust handling, all while keeping the experience approachable for users who may have never used a crypto wallet before.

**The problem it solves**

Splitting shared expenses is still mostly manual. One person pays the full bill, calculates everyone's share, tracks down wallet addresses, and chases each participant individually. The result is delayed payments, calculation errors, and no clear view of who's actually settled up.

**SmartSplit** turns this into a single coordinated, non-custodial payment workflow on Sui. Users connect their wallet, select friends or a saved community, resolve recipients by SuiNS name instead of raw addresses, attach a receipt, and choose an equal or custom split. One approved transaction then pays every recipient atomically. For cases where someone has already covered the full bill themselves, SmartSplit also supports payment requests, so the flow works whether the group is paying together upfront or reconciling after the fact.

**PAYMENTS & STABLECOINS**

SmartSplit directly addresses how people send, receive, and coordinate money on Sui by turning Sui's programmable transaction model into a genuine one-to-many payment primitive: a single wallet-approved transaction pays every recipient at once, atomically. Either the entire group payment succeeds, or none of it does. That guarantee is the core of what makes this a real payments product rather than a UI wrapped around individual transfers.

The project also covers the receiving side, not just the sending side. Users can record who owes them, notify participants through the coordination layer, and let each recipient approve their own payment independently from their own wallet, closer to how real group payments actually unfold.

The current demo runs on Sui Testnet with SUI as the settlement asset, and the same workflow is built to support stablecoins as the transferred asset with no structural change, making SmartSplit applicable well beyond dinner bills: to group purchases, shared subscriptions, community pooled expenses, and everyday multi-party money movement.

**Challenges we ran into**

Technical Challenges Faced
1. Gonka Router API Integration — Implementing API authentication, request formatting, and communication with the Gonka inference gateway.
2. AI Model Reliability — Handling model failures such as HTTP 524 errors, malformed JSON, missing response content, and max_tokens termination.
3. Multi-Model Consensus — Designing a system that sends the same claim to multiple AI models and reliably handles agreement, disagreement, and failed models.
4. Truth Score Algorithm — Designing and implementing a scoring system that combines model confidence, consensus, evidence coverage, and reliability into a 0–100 score.
5. Evidence Retrieval & Ranking — Retrieving relevant evidence from external sources, filtering unusable results, and ranking the strongest evidence before sending it to the AI models.
6. Claim Extraction — Automatically extracting the core factual claim from articles and user-submitted content before verification.
7. Multi-Platform Data Integration — Handling different data structures and APIs from Reddit, X/Twitter, YouTube, Bilibili, Xiaohongshu, and web search, then normalizing them into a common format.
8. URL Content Extraction — Building platform-specific URL detection and content extraction, including dealing with Reddit's post structure and identifiers.
9. Backend–Data Service Communication — Connecting the Express backend to the separate Data service and validating responses between the two services.
10. Production Deployment Constraints — OpenCLI and browser-based integrations worked locally but some failed on Render because the required Browser Bridge/Chrome environment was unavailable.
11. Performance & Concurrency — Managing the high latency of retrieving evidence and running multiple AI models while preventing too many operations from running simultaneously.
12. Error Handling & Validation — Building safeguards throughout the pipeline to prevent invalid input, bad API responses, missing evidence, failed models, and malformed verification results from breaking the system.

**The problem it solves**

🎯 **Problem**
Information is fragmented across news websites, social media platforms and other online sources. Users need to switch between platforms, repeat searches, and compare conflicting claims to understand what is happening. This fragmentation creates several challenges:

1. Information overload: Too much content competes for attention.
2. Information gaps: Important developments may reach some people earlier than others.
3. Missed updates: Relevant information can disappear inside fast-moving feeds.
4. Misinformation: It is difficult to distinguish verified facts from rumors, opinions, or manipulated content.
5. Fear of missing out (FOMO): Users feel pressure to monitor multiple platforms continuously.
6. Time-consuming verification: Checking sources, dates, context, and competing claims requires significant effort.
7. Algorithmic filter bubbles: Platform feeds may prioritize engagement rather than relevance, accuracy, or completeness.

💡 **Solution**
InfoSauce is an AI-powered personal information radar that brings discovery, monitoring, summarization, analysis, and verification into one intelligent hub. It can gather relevant information from multiple sources, remove duplicates, highlight meaningful updates, and present the results in a clear and organized format. Instead of searching across numerous platforms, users can use InfoSauce to:

1. Discover the latest information in one place.
2. Track topics continuously and receive relevant updates.
3. Generate concise summaries of lengthy content.
4. Compare how different sources report the same event.
5. Trace important claims back to their original sources.
6. Identify conflicting information and missing context.
7. Reduce noise while avoiding important missed updates.

**🤖 Gonka Router**
InfoSauce uses Gonka Router as its AI-powered verification layer, sending extracted claims together with ranked evidence to multiple Gonka-hosted AI models for independent fact-checking. Their results are then compared through a multi-model consensus system, where disagreements are treated as uncertain, before InfoSauce calculates a Truth Score from 0–100 using model confidence, consensus, evidence coverage, and reliability. The system also returns the models' reasoning, supporting evidence, and Gonka Request IDs to provide a transparent and traceable verification process.

By combining multiple AI models, relevant external evidence, consensus-based verification, and confidence-aware scoring, InfoSauce aims to produce a more reliable and robust fact-checking result than relying on a single AI model alone.

**AI For Society**

InfoSauce fits the **AI for Society** challenge by using Gonka Router's decentralized AI inference to help people identify misinformation and make more informed decisions online. Our system extracts claims from news and social media content, retrieves relevant evidence, and cross-verifies each claim using multiple Gonka-hosted AI models before generating a transparent Truth Score, reasoning, evidence, and Request IDs. By combining multi-model consensus with evidence-based verification, InfoSauce helps users distinguish trustworthy information from potentially misleading content, reducing the risk of misinformation spreading and contributing to a more informed and digitally resilient society.

**The problem it solves**

# RICE — Reliable Insurance Claim Engine

*Insured, verified, paid — without the wait.*

## Inspiration

Medical insurance claims move through hospitals, insurers, third-party administrators, and payment institutions that each keep their own records of the same claim — leading to slow reconciliation, disputes over what was actually approved, and patients left waiting without a clear, shared source of truth. For someone waiting on a claim decision, that delay isn't just an inconvenience — it can be the deciding factor in whether they get life-saving treatment when they need it.

## What it does

RICE is a shared coordination layer for medical insurance claims. Every institution — hospital, TPA, insurer — works off the same claim lifecycle instead of reconciling separate records after the fact:

1. **AI verification for medical insurance claims**, via the Gonka Router — a plausibility check that produces a Truth Score, a reasoning trace, and a traceable request ID, shown transparently at every point a decision is made.
2. **Automated approval and payment for validated claims**, via smart contracts on Sui — claims that clear both the policy's coverage rules and the AI trust threshold settle automatically, with gas sponsored so no party needs to hold SUI to participate.
3. **Auditing for claim status, verification, and reasoning on Sui's blockchain network** — immutable, distributed-ledger records of the claim lifecycle that every participating institution can independently verify, without needing to trust any single party's internal database.

**The problem it solves**

# GONKA AI Fact Checker

### Verify claims. See the evidence. Prove the result.

GONKA AI Fact Checker is a decentralized AI-powered fact-checking application.

It helps you verify whether a claim or article is **true, false, misleading, or unverified**.

Instead of relying on a single AI model, the system uses three different AI agents to debate the claim.

## 🔍 How It Works

### 1. Submit a Claim

Enter either:

* A text claim
* A public HTTPS article URL

If you submit an article, the system extracts the readable article content automatically.

### 2. Gather Evidence

The system analyzes the claim and can search for additional real-time sources.

Article content, search results, and model-provided references are collected as supporting evidence.

### 3. AI Debate

Three AI agents independently play different roles:

* **Pro Agent — Kimi:** looks for evidence supporting the claim.
* **Con Agent — DeepSeek:** looks for evidence against the claim.
* **Judge Agent — MiniMax:** compares both sides and makes the final decision.

### 4. Gonka Verification

All AI model requests are routed through the **Gonka Router**.

Each successful request produces a unique **Gonka Request ID**, allowing the AI inference process to be traced and verified.

### 5. Final Verdict

The system combines the three-agent results into a final verdict:

**TRUE · FALSE · MISLEADING · UNVERIFIED**

It also generates a **Truth Score from 0–100** and a confidence score.

### 6. Understand the Result

The result includes:

* Final conclusion
* Truth Score
* Confidence
* Pro / Con / Judge summaries
* Evidence and references
* Reasoning metrics
* Risk warnings
* Model request IDs

Metrics include factual accuracy, source quality, logical consistency, neutrality, temporal consistency, and model consensus.

## ⛓️ On-Chain Proof

Once a verification is eligible, the result can be permanently attested on **Arbitrum Sepolia**.

The system creates a cryptographic hash of the claim and prepares the verification evidence for **IPFS**.

You can connect an EVM wallet such as MetaMask and submit the result to the **TruthRegistry** smart contract.

The on-chain record stores the claim hash, Truth Score, verdict, Gonka Request IDs, IPFS metadata, attester, and timestamp.

After the transaction is confirmed, anyone can verify the attestation from the blockchain.

## 📊 Live Dashboard

The application can also display recent on-chain fact-checking attestations directly from the TruthRegistry contract.

This makes verified results transparent and publicly traceable.

## 💡 Why It Matters

GONKA AI Fact Checker combines:

**Multi-Agent AI Debate**

* **Gonka Inference Proof**
* **Evidence & Reasoning**
* **IPFS Storage**
* **Blockchain Attestation**

The goal is simple:

> **Don't just tell people what is true. Show them why — and let them verify the proof.**

**Challenges we ran into**

The trickiest bug we hit wasn't in the AI logic — it was a **silent data-integrity bug in our on-chain attestation pipeline**. Two files responsible for hashing the same claim text had quietly drifted apart: our production endpoint was hashing with SHA-256, while another module used Keccak-256 — the algorithm Solidity actually uses under the hood. Both ran without errors, so nothing failed loudly. We only caught it by inspecting an attestation certificate directly and noticing the "Claim Hash" field rendering two different values side by side, meaning the hash we were verifying and the hash actually stored on-chain weren't the same thing.

Digging further, we found the root cause: the project had two parallel backend implementations, and one had been edited without the other keeping up. The drift wasn't limited to hashing either — the contract was deployed on Arbitrum Sepolia, but leftover strings elsewhere still referenced a different chain, and even a different attestation protocol we'd already decided not to use.

We fixed it by establishing a **single source of truth** instead of patching each occurrence individually: one shared hashing function matching Solidity's Keccak-256, one shared chain-config constant imported everywhere rather than hardcoded per file, and deprecating the unused backend entirely so future edits can't silently diverge again. It was a good reminder that in a system whose whole pitch is verifiable, tamper-evident data, an internal inconsistency is just as damaging as a wrong AI answer — so we now treat "does this value match everywhere it's displayed" as its own test case, not just something to eyeball.

**Challenges we ran into**

## Challenges I ran into

### 1. Challenge One: Designing the Smart Blood Allocation System

One of the main challenges was designing an allocation system that could make meaningful decisions instead of simply selecting the first available blood unit. The system needed to consider blood compatibility, availability, expiry dates, FIFO prioritization, and the distance between hospitals.

**How I solved it:**
I developed a rule-based Smart Allocation Engine that evaluates these factors before selecting and recommending suitable blood units. This allowed the system to prioritize compatible and available units while also considering expiry and proximity.

---

### 2. Challenge Two: Managing the Blood Lifecycle

A blood unit can go through multiple stages, including registration, availability, reservation, transfer, delivery, and issuance. Managing these transitions without allowing invalid actions was challenging.

**How I solved it:**
I implemented structured status transitions and workflow validation. Each stage has defined actions, helping ensure that blood units move through the correct lifecycle. An audit trail was also added to record important changes.

---

### 3. Challenge Three: Handling Inter-Hospital Transfers

Coordinating blood transfers between hospitals required clear control over which hospital could perform actions such as approving, dispatching, and confirming delivery.

**How I solved it:**
I designed a transfer workflow with defined stages and role-based access controls. This helped ensure that actions were performed by the appropriate hospital and that the transfer status could be tracked throughout the process.

---

### 4. Challenge Four: Connecting the UI to Real Data

During the early stages of development, some parts of the dashboard relied on simulated or hardcoded data. This made the application look functional without fully representing the actual backend workflow.

**How I solved it:**
I gradually connected the frontend to the backend and database so that inventory, SOS requests, transfers, and other system information could be retrieved and updated through the actual application workflow.

---

### 5. Challenge Five: Implementing QR/RFID Tracking Without Hardware

The project required a way to track individual blood units, but using physical RFID hardware would add additional complexity and dependency on external devices.

**How I solved it:**
I implemented a software-based QR/RFID identification workflow using unique identifiers for each blood unit. This allowed the complete tracking workflow to be demonstrated without requiring physical hardware, while keeping the system extensible for future integration with actual QR scanners or RFID devices.

---

### 6. Challenge Six: Preventing Blood Wastage

Simply tracking blood inventory was not enough. The system also needed to prioritize blood units that were closer to expiry to reduce unnecessary wastage.

**How I solved it:**
I incorporated FIFO and expiry-based prioritization into the allocation workflow. When suitable blood units are available, the system can prioritize older or earlier-expiring units where appropriate.

**The problem it solves**

## The problem it solves

Blood management across hospitals can be slow and fragmented, especially during emergencies. Hospitals may have limited visibility into the availability of compatible blood at nearby facilities, while manual coordination, delayed inventory updates, and inefficient tracking can increase response time and contribute to blood wastage.

**HAEMO/CORE** provides a centralized platform that helps hospitals manage and coordinate blood inventory across a connected network.

It can be used to:

* Monitor the availability of different blood groups across multiple hospitals.
* Raise and manage emergency blood requests when required units are not available locally.
* Identify suitable blood units based on compatibility, availability, expiry dates, FIFO prioritization, and hospital proximity.
* Track blood bags throughout their lifecycle using QR/RFID-based identification workflows.
* Manage inter-hospital blood transfers from allocation and dispatch to delivery.
* Reduce wastage by identifying and prioritizing blood units approaching their expiry date.
* Monitor cold-chain conditions and flag potential storage issues.
* Analyze blood usage patterns and support future demand planning.
* Maintain a clear audit trail of important actions and blood movement.

By bringing these processes into a single platform, HAEMO/CORE makes blood management more organized, traceable, and efficient while helping hospitals respond more quickly to time-critical blood requirements.

### Avtar.ai

> Meter every call. Settle once on Base.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Ethereum](https://img.shields.io/badge/Ethereum-333333?style=flat-square) ![zkSNARK](https://img.shields.io/badge/zkSNARK-333333?style=flat-square) ![groth16](https://img.shields.io/badge/groth16-333333?style=flat-square) ![BASE](https://img.shields.io/badge/BASE-333333?style=flat-square) ![x402](https://img.shields.io/badge/x402-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Agent-to-agent API payments have no workable settlement layer at the volume agents actually operate at.

On-chain per call is too expensive. An agent buying weather data, a price feed, a translation is each call is worth fractions of a cent, but a Base transaction costs real gas regardless of what it's for. Settling every call on-chain means the fee dwarfs the price. Nobody does that.

Off-chain invoicing has no enforcement. The alternative is meter calls, bill monthly, trust the total — works between humans who have relationships and recourse. It doesn't work between autonomous agents transacting with counterparties they've never dealt with before and have no legal claim against. There's nothing stopping either side from disputing the number afterward, and no cheap way to prove who's right.

What exists in between (x402) only solves discovery and per-call authorization — a provider quotes a price, a consumer presents payment, the call proceeds. It doesn't solve the settlement problem: paying per call is exactly the on-chain-cost problem above, restated.

Avtar.ai closes that gap. The consumer locks escrow once. Calls are metered locally against it — no transaction, no signature, no gas per call. When the channel closes, one Groth16 proof establishes exactly what's owed, and one transaction pays the provider and refunds the rest. The proof is what replaces trust: the amount is provably correct without either party needing to believe the other's ledger, and without publishing the call count, the rate, or what the calls were for.

So the shape of the problem is: agents need to pay each other at machine speed and machine volume, with cryptographic settlement instead of either prohibitive gas costs or unenforceable trust 

## Disclosure

The settlement design which is meter off-chain, prove the total with Groth16, settle
once was first built and proven out on Stellar/Soroban before being adapted for Base. Everything in this repository is a from-scratch implementation for Base: new Solidity contracts, a new TypeScript SDK, a new Foundry test suite, and a rewritten circuit
address-binding scheme (BN254 hi/lo limbs in place of 32-byte Stellar
strkeys). No Soroban code, dependency, or artifact is present here.

**Challenges we ran into**

1.⁠ ⁠A stale proving key silently broke every settlement. The verifier is deployed immutably into the escrow's constructor, generated from a specific proving key. When the local key got regenerated, every proof came back a bare InvalidProof() — no clue why. We traced it to a bytecode diff between the committed verifier and what was actually deployed, then redeployed the full stack from the matching key.

2.⁠ ⁠Public RPC endpoints disagreed on account state mid-transaction. sepolia.base.org load-balances across nodes that don't agree on nonces, so opening a channel (three transactions in a row) would fail partway with nonce too low — a transient infra issue that read like a client bug. Fixed by switching to a steadier endpoint and adding a retry that reads the nonce the chain's own rejection names, instead of re-querying an inconsistent source.

3.⁠ ⁠Solidity and TypeScript had to encode addresses identically, with no automatic check that they did. BN254 field elements can't hold a full address, so each one is split into hi/lo limbs on both sides of the stack independently. A one-character drift between the two implementations would fail silently at settlement, not at compile time. Solved with a shared test vector that pins both implementations to the same expected output, so a mismatch fails in CI.

4.⁠ ⁠The escrow contract has no per-channel balance — only per-depositor. A dashboard trying to show "how much is locked for this channel" was actually reading the depositor's total pooled balance across every channel they'd ever opened, which looks right until two channels are open at once. Fixed by sourcing the per-channel figure from the agent's own session state, since the chain genuinely doesn't track it.

**Private Wallets and Payments**

## Why this track

Paying per API call on-chain would leak how often an agent is used, what it costs, and how much moved. avtar.ai hides that traffic:

- Open: approve USDC, pin terms, deposit escrow.
- Meter: thousands of HTTP calls, none of them a transaction.
- Settle: one USDC payout, capped by escrow. Call count and rate are not public signals in a way that reconstructs the session log. Usage volume and pricing never go on-chain.

Sender, recipient, and amount of each call are not published. Observers see a channel open and a later settlement, not the commercial graph between agents. That is the payment-privacy property this track asks for, applied to agent-to-agent APIs rather than a retail wallet UI.

**Private AI on Ethereum**

## Why this track

Avtar.ai is an AI agent commerce stack whose settlement is a Groth16 proof on Base.

A consumer agent picks tools (weather, crypto price, translation, or real function-calling when an OpenAI key is set), meters each call off-chain over x402, then produces a cryptographically verifiable close: `settle(a, b, c, publicSignals)` checks the proof, the registry confirms the parties, a nullifier stops replay, and the escrow pays out.

The model never has to leave a device for the privacy claim to hold. Prompts, tool names, and call count stay off-chain. What Ethereum sees is a proof of what is owed, matching this track's requirement for an output that is cryptographically verifiable on-chain.

Deployed on Base Sepolia with a working dashboard that shows the live meter and the thirteen public signals.

**Overall**

## Why overall

This is a shipped privacy app, not a slide deck:

- Solidity escrow, agent registry, and Groth16 verifier on Base Sepolia
- TypeScript agents that open channels, meter over x402, prove, and settle
- Next.js dashboard for the live meter and the thirteen public signals
- e2e path: open, meter, prove, settle (local anvil and testnet)

Privacy is the mechanism: call volume never hits the chain, and settlement is one proof. Technical depth (circuit public signals, immutable verifier, nullifier, address packing) plus a usable UX (chat, meter tape, settle button) is what this prize is for.

[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/rime-a6fc) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/adhithyaragavan/rime) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://vimeo.com/1220733802?share=copy&fl=sv&fe=ci) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Road%20to%20Devcon%20--%20NITK%20Surathkal-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://road-to-devcon-nitk-surathkal.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> ANTI AI TAMPERING

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Configfs-tsm](https://img.shields.io/badge/Configfs--tsm-333333?style=flat-square) ![IntelTDX](https://img.shields.io/badge/IntelTDX-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

When an AI agent executes critical operations accessing funds, signing transactions, or managing sensitive data there is no trustless way to verify that its code hasn't been tampered with, that it's running on genuine secure hardware, or that its security posture is current

**Challenges we ran into**

The hardest bug was invisible to every unit test.

Our AgentRegistry contract calls Automata's DCAP verifier to validate TDX hardware quotes. We had 20 passing Foundry tests but the first real deployment silently failed every time with "execution reverted for unknown reason" and zero decodable error data.

The root cause: we had declared verifyAndAttestOnChain as view in our interface. Automata's real function is external payable  it writes state. Solidity compiled our call as a STATICCALL, which the EVM silently reverts the moment the callee touches storage. No revert data. No useful error. Three different RPC providers, same result.

We diagnosed it by splitting the call: calling verifyAndAttestOnChain directly from an EOA (no STATICCALL restriction) succeeded; calling certify() from our contract failed every time. One word change removing view fixed it. We then made the mock's callCount actually increment, so this class of bug fails a unit test if it ever regresses.

Getting TDX attestation right on real hardware was the second challenge. The report_data mode (raw vs sha256), the exact byte offset of report_data in the quote (568), and whether Automata's verifier would actually accept a real quote none of these could be confirmed from documentation alone. We had to spin up a GCP c3-standard-4 TDX Confidential VM, pull a real quote via configfs-tsm, and verify each assumption empirically against the live on-chain verifier

**Private AI on Ethereum**

Rime is built across five interconnected tracks:

Shared Core (packages/shared) Defines the canonical manifest schema, deterministic hashing, and thereport_data commitment encoding that every other layer depends on.

Scanner (packages/scanner) Walks the dependency tree, runs six security heuristics, and wraps OSV/npm-audit to produce an AuditManifest with a tamper-evident auditHash.

Contracts (contracts) On-chain enforcement via AgentRegistry (TDX quote verification + report_data binding + freshness window) and GatedVault (access gating), deployed on Base Sepolia.

Agent Runtime (packages/agent) Runs inside a TDX enclave, performs a boot-time self-check against the baked-in manifest, and heartbeats certify() on-chain every 25 minutes.

Web Dashboard (web) React status page showing live certificate freshness countdowns and client-side audit hash re-verification against on-chain state

### Aegis
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/aegis-2a33) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/DevanshSharma351/Aegis) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M53P269aTuY) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Road%20to%20Devcon%20--%20NITK%20Surathkal-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://road-to-devcon-nitk-surathkal.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Private by Design. Relentless by Nature.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Docker](https://img.shields.io/badge/Docker-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![FastAPI](https://img.shields.io/badge/FastAPI-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

### 1. An attestation proves what was decided, not what was done

We realized that proving an AI decision doesn't guarantee the executor actually follows it. Our allocation was correctly hashed, attested, and recorded on-chain, but the trading code was still executing a fixed swap.

We fixed this by making `plan_rebalance` derive the trade directly from the attested allocation. It compares current holdings with the target and closes the largest gap. The caller can cap the trade size, but cannot choose the trade direction.

### 2. Finding a model small enough, but good enough

One of the harder parts was finding a model that was small enough to run comfortably inside the enclave while still being capable of making reasonable trading decisions. Larger models gave better reasoning, but increased memory usage and inference time, which isn't ideal for a constrained environment.

We tested smaller models and found that some struggled with basic allocation and reasoning tasks, while larger models were more capable but harder to fit within our constraints. We eventually settled on **Qwen 2.5 3B**, which gave us a good balance between model capability, inference time, and the resource constraints of the enclave.

### 3. Making private settlement observable enough to debug

Shielded transactions are great for privacy but make debugging much harder because you can't simply look at a public wallet balance and see what happened. We had to build our own execution checks around transaction receipts, events, and shielded-state updates so the system could verify that a trade actually settled without exposing the portfolio itself.

### 4. Testnet has no private mempool to hide in

We built private transaction submission to prevent swaps from sitting in the public mempool, but found it wasn't useful on Sepolia because there are effectively no MEV builders there. We sampled **60 blocks and found zero MEV-builder blocks**, while mainnet had **22 of 30**.

So Aegis chooses the submission route based on the chain: **private on mainnet, public on Sepolia**, while reporting the actual execution price and surrounding swap activity instead of claiming protection that the network can't provide. The **unshield → swap → reshield** process remains atomic either way.

**The problem it solves**

## What Aegis is

Aegis is an **automated crypto trading agent**. You deposit funds, and on a schedule it reads market data, decides how to split your portfolio across five assets, and makes the trade that moves you closest to that target. A robo-advisor, essentially.

Two things make it different from every other trading bot:

- It runs inside a **secure enclave**, a hardware-isolated part of the processor that can produce a cryptographic receipt proving exactly which code and which AI model produced a decision. That receipt gets written to a smart contract before any money moves.
- It trades inside a **shielded pool (Railgun)**, where balances are encrypted commitments rather than public numbers. Your positions never appear on the blockchain.

## Why that combination matters

Most trading bots are a black box with a Twitter account. You hand over funds, get a performance chart, and take the operator's word that the strategy is what they claimed. Nothing stops them from swapping the model out or rewriting the story after a bad week.

The obvious fix is to put the bot on-chain, where everything is public and verifiable. But that trades one problem for a worse one: your entries, your sizing, and eventually your whole strategy become a public document that anyone can read and trade against.

So you're stuck picking between **trustworthy but exposed** and **private but unverifiable**.

**Aegis gets both. You can verify the agent did what it said. You can't see what it holds.**

## Who'd use it

- **A DAO or small fund** whose members need the treasury strategy to be auditable, without publishing every position to competitors.
- **Anyone delegating to a bot without handing over custody.** The agent signs with a key restricted to one function on one contract with zero ETH attached — and that contract has no ability to move a token. It's not that we trust it not to steal; **it structurally can't.**
- **Users who need compliance without surveillance.** Every trade passes a sanctions-list check before it can execute, proving the funds aren't tainted without revealing which funds they are.

**Private DeFi & Mempools**

Trades use Railgun's shielded pool, with unshield -> swap -> reshield executed atomically.

**Private AI on Ethereum**

An LLM makes portfolio decisions inside a TDX-simulated trusted environment, with the model weights included in the attested image. Each decision is bound to an attestation quote and recorded on Ethereum.

**Overall**

Aegis combines private compute (TEE), private state (Railgun), and public verifiability (on-chain attestations) into a usable application. Every privacy claim is either verified or explicitly disclosed.

### Proofsure
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/proofsure-d272) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/mohdrazeen101106/ProofSure-new) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R6tSP8Qp4pM) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Road%20to%20Devcon%20--%20NITK%20Surathkal-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://road-to-devcon-nitk-surathkal.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Insurance without exposure

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

**Technical/integration challenges**

*Reconciling two independently-designed pieces.* Person A's real ZK circuit used a different public-input structure than the contract originally assumed, 5 values instead of 4, hospitals identified by BabyJubJub public keys instead of Ethereum addresses, payouts in paise instead of wei. HealthInsurancePolicy.sol had to be substantially rewritten to match, while preserving a backward-compatible legacy path for the old test suite.
*Bridging an off-chain currency to on-chain value*. The circuit proves amounts in Indian paise (integer math, no oracle dependency inside the proof itself), but settlement happens in ETH. Solved with a Chainlink price feed doing the paise→wei conversion after verification, so the proof never depends on live price data.
A soundness gap in the circuit itself. The deductible, co-pay, and coverage-limit values used inside the ZK proof are private circuit inputs, the contract has no public signal to check them against the policy's actual on-chain terms. This means a proof could currently be built against fabricated deductible/coverage numbers and still verify. Not yet fixed, needs either exposing those values publicly or committing to them cryptographically.
*A front-running vulnerability in the legacy settlement contract*. ClaimPayoutChainlink.sol's settleClaim let any caller name an arbitrary beneficiary address, meaning a public proof sitting in the mempool could be front-run by someone else redirecting the payout to themselves. Turned out to be dead code (not called from anywhere in the deployed path), but was a real design flaw caught during review.
*Constructor signature drift breaking the test suite.* Adding the Chainlink price feed changed HealthInsurancePolicy's constructor from one argument to two, and the existing test fixture wasn't updated, all 13 tests failed at the deploy step until the fixture was fixed.
*Non-ceremony trusted setups on both ZK pipelines*. Both the claim circuit's Groth16 zkey and the premium pipeline's KZG SRS were generated locally rather than via a real multi-party ceremony, a known, disclosed limitation rather than a "real" trust-minimization guarantee.

**Team/scoping challenge**

*Correctly framing what problem is actually being solved*. The initial instinct, that ZK proofs prevent an insurer from secretly overcharging on premiums, turned out to be legally redundant (contract law already covers that). The real, sharper insight (from Aditya) was that the actual value is on the claims side, removing an insurer's discretion to deny a legitimate claim. That reframing changed the whole pitch.
Tracking what's actually built vs. designed-but-missing. At one point the premium/underwriting side looked completely unbuilt, no model, no proof pipeline, nothing. A later delivery (the EZKL FastAPI backend) closed that gap.

**The problem it solves**

**Health insurance has a trust problem that costs people their privacy, their money, and their time.**

Today's system forces an impossible trade-off, i.e., to get coverage at all, you must surrender your raw medical records to insurers, data that then sits in centralized databases vulnerable to breaches, and can be used to price against you. Then, when you actually need care, claims crawl through weeks of manual adjudication, where legitimate claims get rejected behind non-transparent processes no patient can audit. The entire industry runs on the mistreated assumption that someone must see your private data in order to trust you.

**ProofSure removes that assumption entirely by replacing trust with cryptographic proof.**

On the **underwriting side**, the pricing model runs locally in the client's browser via ONNX runtime, user's sensitive health inputs never leave the device, and are never persisted anywhere. A zero-knowledge ML proof (EZKL) then demonstrates to the insurer that the premium was computed honestly using their exact approved model, bound on-chain by its hash so neither side can cheat ensuring patients don't fake inputs and insurers don't secretly swap pricing models.

On the **claims side**, hospitals sign itemized invoices with EdDSA keys authorized on-chain, and a Groth16 circuit proves five facts simultaneously: the hospital is authorized, the treatment is covered, the expense sum is correct, the deductible/co-pay formula was applied honestly, and the payout respects coverage bounds. Zero medical details touch the chain.

Finally, **settlement is automatic** because, the smart contract verifies the proof, enforces nullifier-based replay protection so no invoice can ever be claimed twice, converts INR to ETH through a price oracle, and pays out instantly.

The result is that no medical data breaches because there's no central trove of medical data; no opaque rejections because verification is mathematical; no waiting weeks for payouts. Payouts now happen in seconds.

**Private AI on Ethereum**

ProofSure's premium underwriting pipeline uses AI in a privacy-preserving way that satisfies both paths this track allows. Client-side, the risk model runs entirely locally in the browser via ONNX Runtime Web, so a user's health and financial data never has to leave their device to get an inference. For a determination that needs to be trusted by the insurer, the same model is run through an EZKL proving pipeline, which produces a zero-knowledge proof that the model was executed correctly on the claimed inputs, without revealing the underlying personal data. This proof can be independently verified, giving a cryptographic guarantee of correct AI inference rather than requiring trust in the party running the model.

**Overall**

Beyond the AI component, ProofSure's core claims-settlement system is built entirely on zero-knowledge proofs deployed and verified on Ethereum (Sepolia). When a policyholder submits a claim, they submit a Groth16 proof that the hospital's invoice is authentic, the treatment is covered, the expense math is correct, and the payout matches the policy's deductible/co-pay terms, all without revealing the underlying medical or financial details on-chain. A nullifier prevents the same claim from being paid twice while revealing nothing about the claim's contents. This directly uses Ethereum's privacy primitives to remove a specific, real point of friction in insurance: the discretionary language insurers use to deny valid claims. Rather than privacy as a feature layered on top, it's structural to how the contract decides whether to pay out. Thus, the insurer has no ability to override a proof that verifies correctly.

Team **Stack Underflow** -- Mohamed Razeen, Utkarsh Sinha, Aditya Saraswat
